articles.title: Google built a great smart speaker, but Gemini isn’t ready for it
articles.summary: The Google Home Speaker looks great, sounds good, and fits into your smart home nicely, but Gemini isn’t the assistant we’ve been waiting for.
articles.body: Smart speakers have spent the past few years searching for a compelling second act. Beyond music, timers, and controlling your lights, they’ve struggled to justify taking up space on the kitchen counter. AI promised to change that. Amazon debuted its new hardware powered by a revamped Alexa last fall, and now it’s finally Google’s turn. The Google Home Speaker is the company’s first new smart speaker in six years and its first “built for Gemini.” After years of neglect, Google appears to be finally getting serious about the smart home — again. The new speaker is the clearest sign yet. Gemini for Home, however, still feels unfinished. [Product: Google Home Speaker | Hardware highs As a piece of hardware, the $99.99 Google Home Speaker is a delightful device. It is the Goldilocks of smart speakers: big enough to sound good, small enough to blend into a room, attractive without drawing attention, and inexpensive enough to consider buying more than one. [Image: The Echo Dot Max, HomePod Mini, and Google Home Speaker. With its clean look, subtle light ring, and soft green shade, the Home Speaker’s design is my favorite of the three. Along with green (jade), pictured, it also comes in red (berry), white (porcelain), and black (hazel). The Home Speaker fits in seamlessly everywhere I tested it: bedside table, kitchen counter, or two paired under the TV. The soft green jade color blends in without being dull. My only disappointment is the lack of a color-matched cable, something both Apple’s HomePod Mini and Amazon’s Echo Dot Max offer. (Oh, and while the cable finally uses USB-C for the wall brick, it’s not removable from the speaker itself, which is an issue if you want a longer cable run or if it ever starts to fray.) There are no visible controls to mar the mesh fabric-covered body, and the activity indicator light ring encircling the base is subtle enough not to be distracting. If it is — for example, when using two speakers under a TV in a dark room — you can turn the light off in settings, something no other speaker offers. The invisible controls, which frustrated me on previous Google speakers, are much more responsive. A tap on top stops or starts the sound or quickly shuts up the assistant, and a tap on either side raises or lowers the volume, with faint glowing white dots to show you hit the right spot. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: As my colleague David Pierce wrote in his hands-on with the speaker, the sound is good for its softball size. I enjoyed listening to music and podcasts on it. As expected, side by side with the Nest Audio — Google’s larger, previous-generation speaker, which was also priced at $99.99 — the Home Speaker doesn’t sound as good. The Audio had both a woofer and a tweeter; the new speaker has just a single driver, and its bass is thinner since it’s smaller. But the smaller size makes it easier to find a spot for it around the home. It does offer 360-degree sound, which the Audio didn’t, and it’s a huge upgrade to the smaller, prior-gen Nest Mini. I had two review units, so I was able to test the Home Speaker’s stereo pairing feature, and it was a significant upgrade. At 80 percent volume, the new Taylor Swift song was clear, crisp, and super loud — house-filling loud. Bass, however, is barely there; Bad Bunny and Rosalía’s vocals soar in “La Noche de Anoche,” but when the boom is supposed to come in, it’s more like a bump. [Image: The Home Speaker can act as audio output devices for the Google TV Streamer. But yes, my Sonos Arc sounds much better. It also cost a lot more. Compared to the competition — the $99.99 Echo Dot Max and the now pricier $129 HomePod Mini — the Home Speaker came in a close third on audio quality for me (David preferred it over the Max). Testing Taylor Swift’s “…Ready for It?” on the Max brought a hint more bass and a fuller sound, while the Mini is quieter but cleaner. The Home Speaker is loud and clear and holds its own on mids and vocals, though they stretch a little thin at times, and, as mentioned, the bass falls short — which it does on most speakers this size. This is the first Google smart speaker you can pair with a Google TV Streamer (and only a Streamer) as an audio output. You can use just one, but adding two gets you simulated spatial audio. My experience was mostly good. The sound synced well with no dropouts. Streaming YouTube was great; the voices came through loud and clear. During a Game of Thrones re-watch, the screams of agony were suitably bone-chilling. But watching the World Cup, it sounded like the commentators were talking in a tin can, necessitating a switch back to my (much more expensive) Sonos system. [Video: Smart Speaker Showdown] If you’re just using your TV speakers, a pair of Home Speakers will be an upgrade. But it only works with content played through the Streamer — if you switch to another HDMI input, the audio switches away from the Home Speaker. The Home Speaker also listens well, which is an important ability for a smart speaker. It has three far-field microphones and a neural processing unit that handles background noise. It did well in every scenario I tested, hearing me even from across the room or when it was playing loud music. It was more responsive than the HomePod Mini, but a tad less than the Echo Dot Max. As with the competition, the Home Speaker is a Matter controller, so you can use it to add and control Matter devices through Google Home. It’s also the first Google Home audio speaker that can act as a Thread border router. (It’s on Thread 1.3 for now, but Google tells me it’s working on supporting Thread 1.4, which will make it easier for Thread border routers from different manufacturers to work together.) Software lows [Image: If you’re considering a Home Speaker, the hardware is the main reason to buy one. On the software side, Gemini for Home — Google’s new smart home voice assistant powered by Gemini models and designed to be more conversational, more useful, and smarter — works on all Google Home speakers. In my testing, it was mostly the same experience on the Nest Audio, Nest Hub (2nd gen), and Nest Hub Max. That’s good news — Google isn’t locking its newest AI features to new hardware. But it also means there’s little reason to upgrade to the new speaker if you’re happy with what you have. --- Google Home Speaker specs * Price: $99.99 * Subscription: Starting at $10 a month, up to a 6-month free trial included * Colors: Jade, berry, hazel, porcelain (jade and berry US only) * Dimensions: 3.4 inches high x 4.2 inches diameter * Power cable: 30W USB-C, 1.5 meters * Memory: 1GB * Storage: 4GB * Processor: Quad Core A55 2.0 GHz with NPU * Speaker: 58 mm full-range driver, 3 far-field microphones, 2-stage mic mute switch * Connectivity: Dual-band Wi-Fi 6, Thread 1.3 border router, Bluetooth 5.4, Matter controller --- As it’s built for Gemini for Home, I had expected the Home Speaker to be noticeably snappier than current models, but it wasn’t any faster than the Nest Audio when responding to commands. Occasionally, some requests that require the cloud took close to 10 seconds, and even local commands like “Turn on the lights” sometimes lagged just as long. While Gemini handled complex requests well — I asked it to turn off one room, set the thermostat, and turn on the lights in another room in one sentence — it took 10 seconds to do so. Alexa Plus completed the same request in under three. (To be fair, Alexa used to be painfully slow, but it has improved substantially.) Speed aside, Gemini was very good with natural conversational control. I could say “Hey Google, I’m cooking and I don’t want to get too hot,” and it knew to turn down the AC. “Hey Google, it’s too dark in here,” and it brightened the lights. When I said I thought there was someone outside, it offered to show my camera feed on a smart display and check my locks. These feel like genuine quality-of-life improvements because they make voice control easier. [Video: Gemini for Home] I like that you don’t have to repeat “Hey Google” during the same conversation, but Gemini has the memory of a goldfish. While following a recipe, Gemini started walking me through making a cherry tomato pasta sauce until I paused too long and it completely lost the thread. Gemini Live fixes some of this by keeping the conversation open until you tell it to stop and remembering previous chats. But this experience feels bolted on. You invoke it differently, by saying “Hey Google, let’s chat,” and unlike Gemini for Home, it can’t take any actions for you (it punts them to Home); it’s just for chatting with. Gemini Live is also behind a $10-a-month Google Home Premium subscription. For general knowledge, Gemini is excellent. It’s substantially better than Google Assistant ever was. I couldn’t stump it with questions about the World Cup’s bewildering brackets, and I was genuinely impressed when I asked which of the matches that had already been played today were worth watching. It summarized them without revealing the score — correctly inferring that I planned to watch them. As a household assistant, it feels less dependable. Mid-cook, I’d ask “When do I add the tomatoes?” only to be told Gemini couldn’t answer until it verified my voice. This same thing happened fairly regularly when adding items to my shopping list — despite Google’s Voice Match being set up. This AI misses the mark The biggest problem with Gemini for Home is that I can’t trust it. Like most LLMs, Gemini is often confidently wrong. It announced the correct title when I asked for “La Noche de Anoche,” then played an entirely different song. Then, when I told it it was wrong, it played another incorrect song. When I asked if I could change the Home Speaker’s voice, it repeatedly insisted it had no alternative voice options; it does. Then the same query on the Nest Hub Max caused it to apparently hallucinate a list of names, including Dimitrix, Impetus, Cameo, and Russell Gethy. (The actual Gemini for Home voices are named after plants.) At one point, it misinterpreted a command to adjust the thermostat as a security request, telling me instead that if I wanted a summary of what was happening in my home, I needed to upgrade to Google Home Premium Advanced. It then proceeded to spell out the upgrade URL. TV controls were the least reliable. Sometimes “Turn on the TV and play YouTube TV” worked. Sometimes Gemini claimed content wasn’t available when it was. Occasionally it announced “Turning on the Living Room TV and launching ESPN,” and then did nothing. I’ve seen similar hiccups with Alexa Plus. They’re part of the current tradeoffs that have come with replacing rigid command-and-control voice assistants with more powerful, flexible LLMs. In the home, when these mistakes happen enough, they undermine the convenience. After spending five days testing Gemini for Home in the Home Speaker, I give the edge to Alexa Plus and its Echo Dot Max. While Gemini for Home’s inference skills were superior in my testing, Alexa Plus has narrowed the gap significantly when it comes to general knowledge. It also has better smart home controls, and I can ask it to set up routines with my voice, something Google doesn’t offer. Both let you use natural language to query and control your home and skip repeating the wake word. But Alexa handles it more smoothly and remembers context and past conversations better. I do prefer Gemini’s voices. My pick, Violet — bright and British — is perfect: no-nonsense without overt personality. I’ve yet to find an Alexa Plus voice I’m comfortable with. What Google Home doesn’t have is ads, something Amazon has introduced to its Echo Show smart displays. But with Gemini for Home, Google is putting some voice assistant and smart home features behind a paywall for the first time. Access to Gemini Live and Help me create, which lets you use natural language to build smart home automations in the app, requires the $10-a-month Standard plan. The $20-a-month Advanced tier adds Home Brief and AI-powered Nest camera features that tie into the Home Speaker. With the Home Speaker, Google built the smart speaker its ecosystem needed: good sound, a cleaner, more modern design, and the radios and processing power to anchor a modern smart home. But Gemini for Home isn’t there yet as an assistant. It’s easier to talk to than Google Assistant ever was, and a lot smarter. But today it’s slow and less reliable. Add the subscription requirement for some of its more interesting features, and the result is a great smart speaker waiting for its AI to catch up. articles.title: AI-created political ads flourish in the lead-up to the midterms. Will voters care?
articles.summary: Some strategists see AI as just another tool to reach voters. Others worry about the optics.
articles.body:
With the midterm elections right around the corner, campaign ads are flooding the airwaves and spreading across social media. And with cheap and easy to use AI tools more readily available, some campaigns are taking advantage of the new technology.

A video shows Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro shooting lightning from his fingertips in a data center. Another video shows Democratic Senate nominee Sherrod Brown at a party where he's overstayed his welcome. And a TV spot from last year's New Jersey gubernatorial race shows a Democratic candidate trading punches with President Trump . While the videos are all real, the images are not: They were all created by AI.

With the midterm elections approaching, voters are seeing more AI-generated ads on TV and social media platforms. While this isn't the first election cycle to see AI ads, the growing technology can create images and graphics for political ads faster and for a fraction of the cost, making it especially useful for campaigns with limited budgets.

But as more ads drop, so too are legal actions from candidates. Democratic Texas state Rep. Vikki Goodwin filed a criminal complaint in September against her GOP opponent Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, alleging since-deleted ads with an AI image of Goodwin violated Texas law. Patrick's campaign said the video ad was "obvious parody." In North Carolina, state Sen. Michael Lee received a cease-and-desist letter in August from his Democratic challenger Jessica Bichler over AI-generated ads that showed faked images of her. And Rebecca Cooke, Democratic challenger to Wisconsin Rep. Derrick Van Orden, sent him a cease-and-desist letter in September alleging a "pattern of posting misleading AI-generated videos that falsely attribute statements to Cooke."

How campaigns are using AI in political ads

According to the Wesleyan Media Project , which tracks political advertising, as of Sept. 4, at least 164 political ads across the country were either produced with or enhanced by AI during the midterm election cycle, costing just under $80 million. Of those, 80% of the ads and 83% of the spending were from Republican candidates or pro-Republican groups, while 11% of the ads and 14% of the spending were from pro-Democratic sponsors. The remainder were a combination of issue ads or ads for independent candidates, the analysis found.

While Republicans seem to be leaning in to using the new technology in campaign ads, Democrats have been more hesitant to embrace it fully. The ways each party has approached using AI in campaigns also tracks with the attitudes about the technology more broadly among voters. The Pew Research Center found that 56% of Democrats said they were more concerned than excited about AI in a June survey, up from 46% in 2023. The same survey found that 49% of Republican respondents were more concerned than excited, down from 59% in 2023.

Eric Wilson is executive director of the Center for Campaign Innovation , which advises conservative campaigns. He describes his organization as a "research and development lab for the conservative movement." Wilson said he believes AI is just one more tool in the technology toolbox that campaigns should use.

"I am an AI maximalist," he said in an interview with Yahoo. "I think it should be used for everything."

He doesn't see AI use as inherently risky for a campaign, unless the candidates themselves aren't particularly interesting.

"If you have nothing to say but you're using AI to say it more, in different ways, that's not a failure of AI, that's a failure of the campaign to be able to articulate a message that resonates with voters," he said. "Are people going to blame AI for that? Sure, but it's really in the mirror that they need to look."

Kate Gage is executive director of the Higher Ground Institute , which advises progressive organizations on how to use technology. In an interview with Yahoo, she said she hears concerns from Democratic candidates that constituents might not like finding out a campaign used AI.

"I think that's something that a lot of us are trying to work on, and there's no silver bullet," she said.

Higher Ground holds "AI open mic" events where campaign strategists exchange tips for using AI in campaigns Those discussions have helped create tools and learnings that others in the party can use.

"I would love a world where people understand this technology enough to be able to speak to the implications of using it, or to have a deeper sense of the challenges or risks," Gage said.

Wilson said he's surprised by how quickly AI has been adopted, at least by the GOP. For campaigns with limited resources, AI has been a big help, Wilson said, allowing them to build their own internal tools and processes to speed things up. This can be particularly useful for mundane, time-consuming tasks like reports and organizing schedules. And those kinds of internal management tools will never make contact with a voter, he added.

But Wilson doesn't think candidates should spend a lot of time explaining their AI practices, either. "Something has gone off the rails with your campaign when you're going out and talking about how you use AI," he said. "I think the best way to think about this is we don't ask candidates if they use spell check. We don't ask if they use machine learning for their ad optimization on Facebook. People are not interested in that process aspect."

Gage said she was hoping to see a little more sophistication in attitudes toward AI by this point. Six months ago, most people she talked with assumed AI involved only creating AI-generated images. But more recently, she says, they are realizing that it's capable of being a source for information.

The data supports her point. An August study by marketing firm Orchestra , which advises Democratic consultants, estimated that people asked AI chatbots roughly 650,000 questions per week about Democrats or Republicans, with ChatGPT and Google AI being used most often.

"I think six months ago, telling someone that people were going to be asking chatbots who to vote for got a lot of shock and confusion from people," Gage said. "And I think we're now in a space where people just understand that to be true. If you're trying to meet people where they are, we need to understand that this is where they are."

She said that now is a good time to show people that AI is "not just a 'nice to have.'"

"You're spending so much time building this campaign and writing your narrative and thinking about how you're communicating and connecting with people. And you need to ensure this is being presented to them in the places where they're looking for that information," she said.

The jury is still out on whether AI ads have directly affected the outcome of political campaigns, but there are more examples to examine now than ever. In Pennsylvania, Shapiro's Republican challenger Stacy Garrity defended her campaign's use of AI , claiming Shapiro's campaign "didn't criticize anything that was in the ad, because it's all true." A Shapiro campaign spokesman called the ad an example of "cheap, dishonest AI."

Separately, in his campaign for New Jersey governor last year, Democratic candidate Josh Gottheimer's campaign used AI to create an ad titled "Born Fighter." The ad showed him in the boxing ring with Trump, and a voiceover that said Gottheimer was "fighting for Jersey to stop Donald Trump's tariffs and chaos." He lost in the Democratic primary to Mikie Sherrill, who went on to win in the general election.

Finally, an ad with an AI-enhanced likeness of former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is running against GOP incumbent Sen. Jon Husted, shows "Brown" at a party that he won't leave. Federal Election Commission records show the ad was paid for by a super PAC with ties to Husted's joint fundraising committee, according

As Cleveland.com notes, the tie on on "Sherrod" switches between colors and patterns, the hands move in ways that aren't realistic and a Happy Birthday sign behind him only has one H, which eventually isn't visible. Brown's campaign commented on the ad calling it af alse advertisement "with fake images."

Cleveland.com found that Federal Election Commission records show the ad was paid for by a super PAC with ties to Husted's joint fundraising committee. But Ohio does not currently have regulations specifically governing the use of AI in campaign ads, and the spot did not include any disclosure about AI use.

Wesleyan found that 69% of the AI ads it reviewed did not include disclaimers that AI had been used, despite laws in some states that require such disclosures. According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, 31 states have laws regulating the use of "deepfakes" — AI-generated or manipulated images, video or audio that falsely depict a person — in political messaging, with some prohibiting certain uses and others requiring a disclosure.

The issue of deepfakes is one area where Republican and Democratic voters agree: A 2025 poll from Ipsos and Boston University found 84% of Americans support protections against AI-generated media that use someone's voice and visual likeness without their permission.

Wilson wrote in a blog post that there are use cases for creating an AI-generated image of an opponent in an ad, such as to highlight something they said that was not on video. But he urges candidates to be transparent about AI use.

"If you're using AI to present something your opponent actually said or wrote, you're not inventing new content. You're creating a new format for it," Wilson wrote , comparing it to issuing a press release that sums up an opponent's stance or idea. "If you're using AI to generate the video, you need to disclose it clearly."

The Democratic National Committee, however, has argued that "video or other content using AI that co-opts another candidate's identity and purports to be the other candidate's own communication," may violate federal election law.

Money connected to the AI industry is also flowing into campaigns this cycle. A New York Times analysis of campaign finance data found that political groups connected with OpenAI and Anthropic, the two leading AI firms in the U.S., have spent roughly $55 million on campaign ads and voter outreach.

Gage, the Democratic strategist, said that in addition to figuring out how to talk to voters about AI, politicians need to get a grasp of AI fundamentals beyond just deciding how their 2026 campaigns may use it.

"Our elected officials are going to be responsible or engaged in very important conversations around regulation, AI safety [and] national security conversations around AI in the next few years," she said. "In my opinion, we need them to understand how powerful this technology can be."

articles.title: Elon Musk throttled Grok Bot after its usage costs became ‘unsustainably high' —as ChatGPT users call OpenAI's new limits the 'end of an era'
articles.summary: Grok Bot was throttled last week because Elon Musk said costs were ‘unsustainably high relative to revenue’
articles.body:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

Grok Bot users recently found they were hitting their usage limits very fast

That's because Elon Musk decided to throttle Grok Bot usage limits

The X owner said Grok Bot costs were "unsustainably high"

If you noticed that you burned through your Grok Bot usage much faster than usual in recent days, there's a reason for that: Elon Musk intentionally limited users' AI agent allowances in the face of "unsustainably high costs." And as you'd expect, a lot of people are unhappy with that.

The revelation came about after an X user pinged platform owner Musk , asking for a Grok Bot reset after they surprisingly hit their 100% usage limit, four days before it was due to reset. They additionally commented that "Normally I don't even reach 100%."

Musk then replied to the post , stating: "The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue."

Many X users seemed irked by the situation, with several saying that their Grok Bot usage had hit the 100% limit while they were sleeping and not using any AI agents. Users claimed their usage had suddenly gone from 50% to 100%, 35% to 78%, and 70% to 100%, all supposedly without using Grok Bot at all.

Elon Musk's comments come amid broader scrutiny of the financial sustainability of many AI products. Tech stocks — including those of many leading AI firms — fell sharply last week as investors grew concerned over the profitability of the industry , with Google revealing that its own AI summaries have hurt its search advertising revenue.

Concerns have also been raised in recent months over the finances involved in many AI companies' offerings. For instance, users of AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude Code can often spend many times more in tokens than they're actually paying in monthly subscriptions, leading to questions over how sustainable many AI business models really are and whether things will need to be adjusted in the near future.

This changing landscape hasn't gone down well with many users, of course. One thread on Reddit dubbed Musk's about-face an "indirect rug pull" of Grok Bot, with features and usage limited in a bid to cut costs.

But it's unlikely that AI producers will be able to subsidize their products' costs to users forever. Usage limits will necessarily need to tighten (as OpenAI quietly announced recently, much to the frustration of users ) and prices will need to increase for these business models to make sense. So don't be surprised if Grok Bot's lower cap is just the first of many big changes looming on the horizon.

articles.title: White House’s Hassett Dismisses Concern Over Financing of AI
articles.summary: White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett dismissed concerns about financing of the artificial intelligence build-out, saying there is ple...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett dismissed concerns about financing of the artificial intelligence build-out, saying there is plenty of capital in the system for such funding.

"It's actually like a really well-financed ecosystem," Hassett said of AI in an interview Monday on CNBC. He was responding to a question about last week's tumble in technology shares, which sent the Nasdaq Composite index to the lowest since July.

Hassett said that it's true that "some companies that maybe have a lot of debt, and you kind of worry about" that. But "there are really, really big-pocketed companies sort of lurking all over the place, owning the equity, owning the debt, perhaps willing to pounce if somebody has trouble."

"There's so much cash in the ecosystem that I think that people should be reassured" even after last week's drop in stocks, he said. "Sometimes things need to go down a little bit" after a big run-up, he said of markets. "But I don't think that there's a risk of a wholesale selloff at all."

articles.title: OpenAI is finally merging ChatGPT's chat and Work tabs | TechCrunch
articles.summary: OpenAI said that ChatGPT and Codex will draw usage from the same allocation pool after this change.
articles.body:
The ChatGPT desktop app can be a confusing piece of software, given that there are ChatGPT and Codex sections, and within the former, there are Chat and Work tabs. With so many options, it’s sometimes easy to forget where you are working and where exactly your project is.

In an apparent effort to address this, OpenAI is now gearing up to merge the Chat and Work tabs within the ChatGPT experience, according to an email sent to users. OpenAI said that initially, this experience will be available to select users for feedback before it is rolled out widely.

“This will enable you to move from exploring an idea to having ChatGPT carry it through, all in one place. You can bring in your files and plugins and ask ChatGPT to build a website, create a presentation, or do things for you on the web, while reviewing and guiding its work. Codex will remain a separate experience in the ChatGPT desktop app,” the email said.

OpenAI also said with this transition, both ChatGPT and Codex will draw tokens from the same allowance pool. It said this change won’t impact most users, but based on usage and model, some folks might need to wait for resets more frequently.

Rival Anthropic merged Claude’s chat and Cowork functions into one screen in September.

articles.title: Omen AI adds liquid know-how in $16 million Aquatic Labs acquisition
articles.summary: Two startups tackling the data center water problem are joining forces in a $16 million deal.
articles.body:
U.S. data centers use 17 to 19 billion gallons of water to cool their hot-running chips each year — and that number is expected to to triple in the next five years, according to the Water Foundation.

That’s an expensive and politically tricky proposition for investors throwing billions of dollars at the challenge of scaling up AI. One way to use less water is to do a better job monitoring the cooling fluids, a task that currently involves sending samples away to a laboratory for tests in a multi-day process.

Omen AI was founded in 2024 to solve that problem. The company is building a real-time sensor to determine whether valves were failing, or if bacteria growth in the system threatened to choke off water flow. After raising a $31 million Series A in June, Omen is now acquiring competitor Aquatic Labs in a $16 million cash-and-stock deal.

The deal came together after Omen founder Zach Laberge was introduced to Aquatic Labs’ CEO Allan Adams by an investor in the filtration space. Both startups were building real-time water sensors with complementary technology: Omen’s sensors looked for elements in the water, while the Aquatic Labs sensor tests its alkalinity.

Putting those two technologies in the same sensor creates a “much richer picture of the water and the fluid,” Adams told TechCrunch, while uniting their vision of automating what had previously been a slow, manual process.

The combination unites two classic species of founder: Laberge dropped out of high school to pursue his first company, which did similar fluid analysis for large construction machines that depend on hydraulics. Adams was an academic, trained as a physicist, who spent much of his career developing advanced ocean sensing technology as an MIT professor and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute researcher before starting his company.

Now, with Adams as the company’s chief science officer, the combined teams are working to integrate both technologies into one sensor, which they expect to have on the market by early next year. Omen’s initial sensors will be monitoring chips pulling in 250 to 300 MW of power by the end of the year, worth about $5 to $7 billion, Laberge told TechCrunch, with the hope of being installed on the equivalent of 1 GW of chips by the end of 2027.

The added value is in uptime: If the fluid system gets out of whack, data center operators typically choose to dump the water rather than risk damage to their expensive equipment. That means shutting down operations until the fluid system is restored, which costs a lot of money. Monitoring lets data center operators use the same fluid for longer, and minimize the costs of a clean up.

Adams hopes to see their technologies have an impact outside of data centers as well, telling TechCrunch that “water goes into data centers, and then it comes out and gets dumped into municipal water, and you want that whole process to happen in a way that’s as safe and responsible as possible — and that means you got to measure stuff.”

AI companies once estimated as much as $4 trillion would be spent on AI infrastructure by 2030, but some investors have grown skeptical of the buildout , sending hyperscaler stocks plummeting in recent days. Omen’s team isn’t worried about shifting sentiment though, since their work comes after a data center has been built.

articles.title: Sam Altman thinks it's 'quite terrible' for your PC to be using memory that AI companies need so badly
articles.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently said it's "quite terrible" that memory is sitting in your computer, rather than being used in AI data centers.
articles.body:
Among the many impacts the AI industry has had on the world in the last several years, the ongoing memory shortage is one of the biggest. OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and other tech giants are gobbling up the world's memory supply to power their data centers, sending prices for consumer electronics skyrocketing . Given that context, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman thinks it's "quite terrible" that you have memory sitting in your computer that AI companies could be using instead.

Altman's comments came in a recent interview with Stripe cofounder John Collison , where he discussed the surge in interest in running open-source AI models on local hardware (like your own PC) rather than relying on big AI companies to handle the processing in the cloud. "From, like, a global allocation perspective, actually it's quite terrible to have everybody, like, have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their computer and being used 5% of the time," Altman said. "Like, you want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment."

Altman's comments have not gone over well online . "He sees anyone owning something for their own personal use as a resource that he's being denied," one Reddit user said on the website's r/Technology board. "Sam Altman is [mad] at resources being used by other people for their own use instead of being used to make him richer," another added . That sentiment carried through most of the comments throughout the thread.

The reason for the backlash is simple: memory (or RAM) is integral to every piece of consumer electronics you own. Everything from your computer to your smartphone, smart thermostat, car, game console and TV relies on memory to work. Modern gadgets simply wouldn't work without it, which is why the current shortage — driven by AI companies eating into the global supply — has driven prices for nearly all consumer tech higher.

We've seen this hit game consoles particularly hard this year. In April, Sony significantly raised prices across the PlayStation 5 lineup, bringing the most affordable model to $600 – up from $400 at launch in 2020. Nintendo and Xbox both followed up with price hikes of their own. PC manufacturers have been heavily impacted as well, with RAM prices climbing more than 500% over 12 months. PC sales have plummeted as a result, falling more than 21% year-over-year in the third quarter of 2026.

The memory price surge shows no signs of slowing either. SK Hynix, a South Korean company that ranks as the world's second-largest memory manufacturer, recently said it expects shortages to last through 2030 . It added that more than half of its production is already booked for the next two years.

AI companies are also under increasing pressure to demonstrate profitability as they prepare to go public. OpenAI is reportedly seeking a $1.25 trillion valuation , though it posted a net loss of $38.5 billion for 2025. Anthropic, largely viewed as OpenAI's largest competitor, recently filed paperwork to prepare to go public , revealing huge spending commitments and operating losses.

articles.title: Elon Musk's answer to Christopher Nolan's Odyssey is 7 minutes of painfully dull AI slop
articles.summary: Elon Musk's AI Odyssey is a spectacular failure, and its ugly origins make it even worse
articles.body:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

Elon Musk wanted to prove that AI could make a better adaptation of Homer's The Odyssey than Christopher Nolan. After months of complaining about Nolan's film, he promised that Grok Imagine would produce a more faithful version of the ancient Greek epic. The first seven minutes have debuted, effectively arguing for leaving filmmaking to people who actually care about telling stories, not pursuing petty bigotries.

The project also has an ugly origin that's worth remembering. Musk's objections to Nolan's adaptation centered heavily on its casting, particularly Black actress Lupita Nyong'o and transgender actor Elliot Page. He accused Nolan of sacrificing historical accuracy to satisfy Hollywood sensibilities, and described the director's casting choices in explicitly racist terms. Ignoring the historical and textual incoherence of his arguments, he promised a full-length AI-generated alternative.

The seven-minute opening episode, produced using Grok Imagine in collaboration with Wonder Studios and director Dev Walker, showcases an astonishing marriage of bad ideas and poor execution, backed by bottomless resources and prejudice.

Watch Episode 1 of our Odyssey series made with Grok Imagine.Let us know in the comments if you'd like a full breakdown of how it was done! Creative collaboration with @WonderStudiosX and director Dev Walker @glumlot_ — @imagine (October 23, 2026) Voir le tweet original

Watch Episode 1 of our Odyssey series made with Grok Imagine.Let us know in the comments if you'd like a full breakdown of how it was done! Creative collaboration with @WonderStudiosX and director Dev Walker @glumlot_

The one positive comment that doesn't ring false is that some of the landscapes look nice and atmospheric, and some shots of ships sailing across the water could pass for outdated video game cutscenes that would have been impressive at the time. Otherwise, Grok's Odyssey resembles a collection of trailer clips from someone who watched Gladiator half-asleep 20 years ago and has looked at the covers of some Greek mythology books.

The dead-eyed Odysseus sounds like someone trying to pretend they are angry the whole time, even when he's talking to the family he supposedly loves. The events that should establish the story's emotional foundation have less emotional depth than a pop-up book.

A human filmmaker and actor could turn Odysseus's departure from his wife Penelope into a moment that haunts the whole film. Grok simply presents the event and moves along, apparently satisfied that the relevant plot point has been included.

That's what makes the comparison with Nolan so embarrassing. Whatever anyone thinks of his films, Nolan understands that cinema depends on controlling an audience's attention and emotions. His movies are constructed around deliberate creative decisions, with performances and editing working together to give individual moments significance. Grok can imitate the appearance of those moments, but the imitation has little weight.

AI keeps getting better, and future models may eliminate many of the visual inconsistencies that currently make AI footage so recognizable. But technical improvement alone won't give a machine the personal experiences or creative intentions that shape meaningful art.

A great film reflects the choices of people who have something they want to communicate. Directors bring their own understanding of the world to a story, while actors draw on human experience to make fictional emotions believable. The best scenes work because somebody understands exactly what the audience should feel and has carefully shaped the experience to produce that response.

That said, a talented human director might use AI to enhance or augment a scene that would otherwise be impossible on a limited budget. But any artistic value would come from the filmmaker's decisions.

But regardless of the intent of Wonder Studios and its team, Grok's Odyssey looks terrible, and the blatant bigotry fueling Musk's comments would make for queasy viewing even if it were somehow comparable to Nolan's epic. Producing seven dull minutes for a fraction of a Hollywood budget doesn't automatically make those minutes an artistic achievement.

The Odyssey and all of its best interpretations have endured partly for what they impart about the very human experience of longing for our loved ones. Those emotions have kept audiences interested for thousands of years. Grok has managed to reproduce some of the costumes and scenery while making the characters feel almost entirely irrelevant.

The AI Odyssey has become a seven-minute reminder of why human creativity matters. For all the technology involved, the most revealing thing about this experiment is how little artistic imagination it contains.

(Bloomberg) -- DeepSeek has unveiled a new option to quickly create custom plugins that help users to tackle a range of complex tasks, the latest move by the Chinese lab to bolster its AI agent offerings.

The Hangzhou-based company showcased ways to make plugins to render 3D models as well as a video editing workbench by providing instructions in plain English, among other examples.

Top AI developers in the US and China are competing to offer more advanced AI agents that can take on work for professionals and everyday users, including writing code, fielding financial research and more. DeepSeek's AI agent is aimed more at developers than casual users.

Earlier this year, DeepSeek created the Harness team to focus on helping build AI agents that can complete with AI coding services — a lucrative area of focus for US firms like Anthropic PBC. DeepSeek dropped an enhanced coding assistant on Saturday that's designed to proactively help resolve issues while requiring minimal human attention.

The term harness refers to the software scaffolding that wraps around a large language model, which enables AI agents to manage more complex tasks.

To better compete with Anthropic and OpenAI, DeepSeek has raised about 100 billion yuan ($15 billion) in its latest fundraising round, one of China's largest-ever, ahead of its initial public offering.

articles.title: OpenAI pitches data center power plants as a way to protect nearby areas
articles.summary: OpenAI is launching a new “Grid Protectors” program that it says will free up power at its data centers during emergencies and extreme weather conditions.
articles.body: In an announcement on Monday, OpenAI says it will pilot its “Grid Protectors Program” at an upcoming data center in Effingham County, Georgia, where the company promises to free up to 1,000 megawatts of power during extreme weather or emergencies, enough to power air conditioners in around 700,000 homes. The announcement comes as opposition to data centers spreads across the US, in response to massive projects that have begun development and construction, frequently with little or no input from local residents. In Utah, residents protested after Box Elder County commissioners signed off on a data center expected to consume more than double the state’s peak electricity demand in 2025, and spread hot air in the desert valley surrounding the data center. Now OpenAI’s approach is to pitch the construction of power plants that feed the electricity required by the new AI data centers it’s building as “a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most.” Several states like Tennessee, Florida, Oklahoma, Oregon, and others have enacted laws that say they will prevent AI companies from passing energy costs on to residents, in addition to moratoriums and other restrictions. This is besides the environmental impacts, as a recent study by the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC) said that powering proposed Texas data center projects could undo decades of air quality gains over just five years. OpenAI, which has switched to calling its AI data centers “compute campuses” in an effort to separate from their poor public reputation, claims it helps reduce costs for customers by operating year-round: “Electricity demand also rises and falls with the seasons, with different regions facing their biggest peaks at different times,” OpenAI’s announcement says. “Our compute campuses need power year-round. With the right agreements, that steady demand can help spread the grid’s fixed costs across more electricity sales, while flexibility lets us reduce demand when the system is busiest.” OpenAI says it’s going to continue working with policymakers and utility services to make “arrangements for our future campus to reduce electricity demand when the grid is under strain.” Along with its data center in Georgia, OpenAI is also partnering with Oracle and SoftBank to build its “Stargate” data centers across the US, including in Shackelford County, Texas; Doña Ana County, New Mexico; and Milam County, Texas.

articles.title: New York Times and other outlets sue web browser Brave over alleged content scraping | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The New York Times is suing privacy-focused web browser company Brave for allegedly scraping the outlet’s copyrighted content and unlawfully distributing it to its own customers, like Anthropic and Perplexity.
articles.body:
The New York Times sued Brave, the 11-year-old, privacy-focused browser company, on Monday, alleging it scraped the outlet’s copyrighted content and unlawfully distributed it to customers the suit names as Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere.

Separately on Monday, the Daily News, the Chicago Tribune, and the Orlando Sentinel filed a similar lawsuit. Both were brought in federal court in Manhattan.

The New York Times, which has also sued OpenAI and Perplexity over similar claims, likens Brave to a “supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content” for AI companies.

“In this way, Brave acts both like a burglar that misappropriates the content of publishers, and an AI ‘fence’ that sells stolen content to third parties,” the suit reads. It says Brave built an index of more than 30 billion web pages using an unidentified crawler, leaving publishers unable to block it.

The suit also targets a Brave browser feature that bypasses paywalls and the company’s practice of blocking publishers’ ads while selling its own.

Founded in 2015, Brave has raised roughly $250 million to date, according to private-market trackers. The Times seeks an injunction and damages.

Brave did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Web host Squarespace lays off 19% of its employees
articles.summary: The website builder said that the job losses are part of a broader restructuring of its organization.
articles.body:
Squarespace, the web company that helps customers build and host their own websites, is laying off about one-fifth of its workforce, in a move that will affect hundreds of jobs.

Jeff Seedman, a public relations specialist representing Squarespace, confirmed the layoffs to TechCrunch. The Verge initially reported the layoffs.

“Squarespace is restructuring its organization and reducing its global workforce by approximately 19%, representing around 300 employees,” said Seedman. “The changes are intended to simplify how we operate, sharpen our priorities and enable the company to move faster as we position Squarespace for its next phase of growth.”

Website building has changed immensely over the last few years as a result of the generative AI boom. “Vibe-coding” website builders, which only require simple prompts from users to spin up functional front-end designs, have largely upended the industry, making it possible for users to create sites with significantly less effort.

These kinds of sites have become an increasingly central part of the website-building business. Last year, web host rival Wix bought Base44 for $80 million . Similar offerings, like Lovable, have generated significant investor interest; Lovable raised a $400 million Series C round in August that valued the company at $13.3 billion. Google also recently launched Stitch , a feature that allows users to swiftly generate user-interface designs.

Squarespace has also begun a big push into AI. In 2024, the company launched an AI tool called Blueprint. The company also recently announced Forma, an upcoming AI native platform, whose waitlist users can join .

Squarespace was founded in 2004 and went public in 2021 at a $10 billion valuation. However, the company struggled in the ensuing years to generate enthusiastic public market interest. Squarespace ultimately decided to go private again by way of a $7 billion private equity deal in 2024.

articles.title: Anthropic warns that it's very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI | TechCrunch
articles.summary: RSI is the point at which AI grows so good at training itself that it spawns a dramatic acceleration of AI capabilities. To the AI doomers, RSI represents the cataclysm from which there is no return.
articles.body:
While much attention has focused on the updated financials Anthropic revealed in its revised S-1A on Monday, (revenue is soaring, but so are expenses), the AI lab dropped another little bombshell in the fine print.

The filing seems to warn that the company is on the cusp of creating a model capable of recursive self-improvement (RSI).

RSI is the point at which AI grows so good at training itself that it spawns a dramatic acceleration of AI capabilities. To the AI doomers, RSI represents the cataclysm from which there is no return, in which AI builds itself into something powerful enough that it slips beyond human control and may be indifferent to the damage it causes while achieving its goals.

To AI enthusiasts, RSI, or some version of AI reliably using itself to improve, represents the technology’s promise, where it becomes a tool of unimaginable productivity, scientific discovery, and more.

Anthropic seems to believe that RSI is both a promise and a peril. It says in the S-1 that it uses AI in its R&D, but it cautions: “Using AI to help build more capable AI could also pose a considerable safety risk, particularly if it sharply accelerates the pace of progress. This is one of the areas covered by our Responsible Scaling Policy, which sets out our plans to monitor and mitigate the risks as we approach what has been termed ‘recursive self-improvement.’”

When the term RSI became popular earlier this year , many believed it was a buzzword or, at best, a goal too hard to achieve, define, or prove.

But on Monday, Anthropic added new statements to its Risk Factors section, saying 1) it has already used AI to develop new models whose leaps in capability it didn’t recognize at the time, and 2) it may soon meet its own internal definition of RSI (bold emphasis ours, below):

In addition, our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures. As a result, we have in the past not identified , and may in the future not identify, a significant acceleration in our rate of development until after it has occurred. For example, our internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.” We have not designated any of our current models as exceeding this threshold, and we continue to assess the underlying data.

In addition, our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures. As a result, we have in the past not identified , and may in the future not identify, a significant acceleration in our rate of development until after it has occurred.

For example, our internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.” We have not designated any of our current models as exceeding this threshold, and we continue to assess the underlying data.

However, Anthropic also said in the filing that none of its models have crossed this RSI threshold yet and that it is promising to keep humans in the R&D process for the foreseeable future. “We do not anticipate being able to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding, if and when that becomes technically possible. Accordingly, we are considering updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development at Anthropic.”

Skeptics might point out that an S-1 functions as both disclosure and marketing, and that claims of being close to a model so powerful that it can build itself could fall into the latter category.

Nevertheless, there’s no question that Claude’s capabilities, especially in terms of coding, math, and cybersecurity, have grow in leaps and bounds this year. If Anthropic thinks the possibility of RSI is close, maybe we should believe it and act — perhaps govern — accordingly.

articles.title: Foto de avião que caiu nos EUA em queda livre foi manipulada com IA | G1
articles.standfirst: Ferramenta de detecção da OpenAI aponta que conteúdo foi fabricado com ferramenta de IA da própria empresa. Conteúdo viralizou depois de queda de aeronave que deixou nove mortos na Flórida neste domingo (dia 1º).
articles.summary: Ferramenta de detecção da OpenAI aponta que imagem foi criada com ferramenta da própria empresa. Imagem falsa circula após queda de avião na Flórida deixar nove mortos no domingo.
articles.body:
É #FAKE que foto de avião prestes a se chocar contra o solo mostre acidente com jatinho nos EUA; imagem foi manipulada com IA — Foto: Reprodução

Circula nas redes sociais uma foto que supostamente mostraria o avião que caiu neste domingo (dia 1º) na Flórida , nos Estados Unidos , imediatamente antes do choque da aeronave contra o solo. É #FAKE .

Publicada no Instagram , Facebook e X , a imagem mostra um jatinho prestes a atingir frontalmente o chão, em uma via cheia de veículos.

Veja dois exemplos de legendas: "Não consigo imaginar o carro vendo aquele jato" ; e "🚨ACIDENTE HORRÍVEL DE JATO PARTICULAR NA FLÓRIDA, EUA!" .

As descrições omitem que se trata de um material fabricado com inteligência artificial (IA), como comprova uma ferramenta de detecção usada pelo Fato ou Fake (veja detalhes mais abaixo) .

O conteúdo viralizou no dia seguinte à queda de um avião em um bairro residencial da Flórida . O Learjet 60, uma aeronave particular, havia decolado do aeroporto de Austin, no Texas, com previsão de pousar nas Bahamas.

As nove pessoas a bordo, inclusive a copiloto, Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, de 20 anos , filha de brasileiros, morreram. Entre as vítimas, estavam quatro integrantes de uma família com crianças duas crianças, de 2 e 4 anos, além de uma babá e duas amigas próximas.

O Fato ou Fake submeteu a imagem ao detector de IAda OpenAI, dona do ChatGPT, que consegue identificar materiais fabricados ou manipulados com modelos da própria empresa. articles.title: Mandando Bem no Enem: professora orienta revisão de Sociologia | G1
articles.standfirst: Luiza Anselmo, do Colégio Nacional, explica como relacionar teoria sociológica, desigualdades, cidadania e direitos à análise da realidade brasileira.
articles.summary: Luiza Anselmo, do Colégio Nacional, explica como relacionar teoria sociológica, desigualdades, cidadania e direitos à análise da realidade brasileira.
articles.body:
Relacionar conceitos sociológicos e situações do cotidiano ajuda a desenvolver a análise crítica para o Enem. — Foto: Imagem gerada por Inteligência Artificial.

Relacionar a teoria sociológica aos dilemas da sociedade brasileira é uma das orientações da professora Luiza Anselmo, do Colégio Nacional, para a preparação para o Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio (Enem) 2026. Com atuação em Filosofia e Ciências Sociais, ela recomenda estudar o papel das instituições, os direitos de cidadania e as desigualdades a partir de situações concretas.

Segundo a professora, a preparação combina conhecimento dos conceitos, leitura atenta e análise crítica. A proposta é compreender como os autores ajudam a interpretar a realidade, em vez de limitar a revisão à memorização de nomes e definições.

“No Colégio Nacional, nós fazemos com que os estudantes aprendam a olhar para a nossa própria comunidade e para o mundo com alteridade e criticidade. Isso muda completamente a forma como as questões são respondidas no ENEM”, afirma Luiza.

Compreenda como as desigualdades se estruturam

Estratificação e mobilidade social estão entre os temas destacados para a revisão. O estudo deve considerar como a sociedade se organiza e quais barreiras interferem nas oportunidades dos diferentes grupos.

A orientação é observar como marcadores de classe, etnia e gênero se relacionam às desigualdades no Brasil. Essa análise ajuda a conectar os conceitos às situações apresentadas nos textos e nos dados das questões.

Relacione cidadania e garantia de direitos

Outro eixo é a construção histórica dos direitos civis, políticos e sociais. Luiza recomenda estudar a Constituição Federal de 1988 e sua relação com a garantia de direitos fundamentais, considerando também a atuação dos movimentos sociais.

O foco é compreender a relação entre direitos reconhecidos e sua efetivação, analisando o papel das instituições e dos poderes públicos. Esse estudo permite discutir cidadania e democracia como processos históricos e sociais, sem reduzir a preparação à memorização de dispositivos legais.

Observe a cultura e os meios de comunicação

Cultura, indústria cultural e diversidade também integram as orientações da professora. A revisão pode explorar a influência dos meios de comunicação de massa na formação da opinião pública e a maneira como diferentes grupos e modos de vida são representados.

Nesse eixo, é importante relacionar a valorização da diversidade cultural à crítica ao etnocentrismo. O exercício de análise exige considerar o contexto das práticas culturais e evitar julgá-las apenas a partir das referências do próprio grupo.

Precarização, informalidade e automação são exemplos de temas para estudar as relações produtivas contemporâneas. A orientação é compreender como as mudanças no mundo do trabalho afetam a organização da sociedade e as condições de vida dos trabalhadores.

Para conectar teoria e realidade, Luiza indica relacionar conceitos de Karl Marx, Max Weber e Émile Durkheim, assim como de Zygmunt Bauman e Lélia Gonzalez, a notícias e reportagens. A proposta é usar essas referências para interpretar os problemas apresentados, considerando a contribuição de cada autor.

Pratique a leitura de dados e do comando da questão

Gráficos e tabelas do Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE) e do Instituto de Pesquisa Econômica Aplicada (Ipea) podem ajudar a observar disparidades socioeconômicas. Na revisão, vale praticar a interpretação desses dados e relacioná-los aos conceitos estudados.

Durante a prova, a professora recomenda ler o enunciado antes do texto, identificar o que ele solicita e observar a fonte. Reconhecer se a questão pede uma definição, uma causa ou uma consequência ajuda a direcionar a leitura e a análise das alternativas.

O mesmo cuidado com a fundamentação vale para a redação. A orientação é evitar explicações baseadas apenas no senso comum e empregar o repertório sociocultural de forma pertinente ao argumento. Para Luiza, compreender a sociedade faz parte de uma formação que ultrapassa o resultado do exame.

articles.title: Apple may try to increase revenue by doing...something with third-party AI apps | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Apple hinted at ways that it could spur revenue through third-party "opportunities" during its Monday night earnings call.
articles.body:
Apple’s services business remains at record levels, but it’s facing growing pressure . The central part of that business, Apple’s App Store, has faced regulatory pressure and a slump in mobile gaming, which have hurt services growth .

However, on Monday’s earnings call, Apple signaled that it may look to boost services revenue through third-party apps. What does that mean, exactly? Unfortunately, it’s not entirely clear.

When discussing how AI could potentially “contribute to revenue growth over time,” Kevan Parekh, Apple’s chief financial officer, said: “On the product side, you know, we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities, and we also feel there’s opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities.”

Parekh did not elaborate on what sorts of opportunities might be available via third-party apps. However, Reuters reported Monday that investors are wondering whether Apple could profit by distributing third-party AI agents through the App Store and taking a cut of the revenue they generate.

Regulatory and legal changes have cut into App Store commission revenue in some markets, even as Apple’s services business as a whole continues to grow. Third-party estimates in August, for example, suggested the company had seen an 18% drop in U.S. commission revenue, with declines also in Brazil and Japan after those countries introduced new regulations. Apple has traditionally controlled payments within its app marketplace tightly, taking a cut of all App Store transactions. But a lawsuit by Epic Games ultimately forced the company to allow apps to redirect users to outside payment systems. Other legal challenges throughout the world have further hampered the business.

During the earnings call, Parekh referenced Apple’s App Store woes and returned to the idea that the company’s service business could expand into new territory.

“We’ve also seen some factors that impacted the performance of the App Store, and during the September quarter, the performance on the App Store was similar to the prior year, and we had a record number of paid subscriptions with double-digit growth for third-party apps on the App Store,” Parekh said. “At the same time, we did see some headwinds in mobile gaming that we’ve talked about before, and expect to see those continue into the summer quarter.”

Parekh added: “As we move ahead, we expect services growth to to be between 8 to 9% [in the December quarter]. This outlook contemplates our best estimates on sequential headwinds, primarily from third-party licensing and the additional half percentage point of foreign exchange I just mentioned.”

TechCrunch has reached out to Apple for more information and will update this story if it responds.

articles.title: Anthropic was founded to answer to humanity. Soon, it will also answer to Wall Street
articles.summary: In 2021, a group of employees at OpenAI left to start a new company focused on the safe development of artificial intelligence. They named it Anthropic, a word that means “relating to humanity.” Later this month, that company is expected to make its debut on Wall Street in what could be one of the largest initial public offerings in history. But the move raises a fundamental question: Can a company put humanity first while also answering to Wall Street?
articles.body: In 2021, a group of employees at OpenAI left to start a new company focused on the safe development of artificial intelligence. They named it Anthropic, a word that means “relating to humanity.” Later this month, that company is expected to make its debut on Wall Street in what could be one of the largest initial public offerings in history. But the move raises a fundamental question: Can a company put humanity first while also answering to Wall Street? The IPO is a monumental development for the AI boom and will put a spotlight on how investors feel about the maker of the Claude chatbot. The stock market debut also marks a new chapter for Anthropic that will test whether it can balance its mission of safely developing AI with the pressures of being a publicly traded company. Anthropic has a special ownership structure designed to help the company stick to its original goals, balance profit growth with its mission and keep investors from staging a takeover. The structure includes a group of trustees who have majority control of the board of directors, as well as a special class of shares that ensures the seven founders own a majority of the general shareholder voting power. With its mission for safe AI and its unorthodox corporate structure, Anthropic’s Wall Street debut can be viewed as a guinea pig for AI frontier labs and how they are received by investors. Public benefit corporation Anthropic is registered as a public benefit corporation, or PBC. These types of companies are legally required to balance the interests of shareholders with the company’s stated mission. It’s different from a traditional company that focuses primarily on maximizing shareholder value. “The governance structure for Anthropic is very unique,” said Gil Luria, head of technology research at financial services firm D.A. Davidson. “They spell it out. They’re very upfront about it.” Anthropic described its “tripartite goals” as a PBC in its S-1 filing: “the pecuniary interest of our stockholders, the best interest of those materially affected by our conduct and the Company Purpose.” Just a fraction of publicly traded companies are PBCs. Patagonia, which is privately held, and eyewear retailer Warby Parker (WRBY) are both PBCs. PBCs can choose what they want to do with corporate profits and invest as much as they want in safety measures. And investors have little power to do anything about it. Anthropic rival OpenAI became a PBC in 2025. “Anthropic is explicit about that, that they believe that there will be instances where they choose not to maximize shareholder value because of the judgments that they make, the board and the leadership team,” Luria said. “Growing the company and enjoying profitability are part of the goal, so it’s not that it’s contrary to the goal,” he added. “It’s just that they’re saying that there may be some cases where that is not the goal, or they seek other goals, even at the expense of growth and profitability.” Anthropic’s seven founders collectively have 50.1% of the voting rights at the company, which means regular shareholders won’t have any say in its operations. This is a variation of a trend in Big Tech companies in recent years that have had structures where the founders retain majority control, like Mark Zuckerberg at Meta and Elon Musk at SpaceX. Long-Term Benefit Trust It’s not just that the founders have majority control. Anthropic in 2023 established the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), which is composed of five subject-matter experts who have no financial stake in the company’s stock. However, they have special non-financial shares with the authority to appoint four directors to the seven-person company board. The LTBT members include Neil Buddy Shah, CEO at the Clinton Health Access Initiative; and Ben Bernanke, a former chair of the Federal Reserve. There is one vacancy in the LTBT that has yet to be filled. “The LTBT may have interests that differ from yours, and it may exercise its power in a way with which you disagree or in a way that may be adverse to your interests,” Anthropic says in a filing with the SEC, referring to shareholders. When a company goes public, there can be more pressure to grow profits and deliver strong results for shareholders. But Anthropic and CEO Dario Amodei have also talked about the risk of AI causing tremendous harm to humanity if placed in the wrong hands. Anthropic’s IPO filing includes more than 90 pages of risk disclosures, varying from how AI can be misused by bad actors to the possibility of existential risk to humanity. “While this Long-Term Benefit Trust has a lot of power, the founders also have a lot of power. But, you know, in both cases, public shareholders don’t have the power,” said Jay Ritter, professor emeritus at the University of Florida and an expert in IPOs. What does this all mean? If there are growing concerns about AI, the founders and LTBT can make decisions for the company that impact the value of shares without any consideration for investors. In theory, it can help the company stick to its mission — but it remains to be seen how the structure will function until an event forces the company to act. Anthropic’s ownership structure won’t matter as much if profits are strong and it follows its mission of developing safe AI. But it will be stress-tested if earnings aren’t as strong as expected, safety issues arise, or disagreements fester between the board, founders or trustees, Luria at D.A. Davidson said. “The strangest aspect of Anthropic’s filing is its corporate governance structure,” Jay Goldberg, senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners, wrote in a note. “We believe this is the largest PBC and the full implications of this structure will take time to become apparent.” “We believe this structure gives the LTBT and the founders effective permanent control of the company,” Goldberg added.
