articles.title: Everything you need to know ahead of Anthropic's IPO
articles.summary: Anthropic made its IPO filing public, so its roadshow could start Nov. 10, with a potential debut targeted for the week before Thanksgiving. Here's everythin...
articles.body:
Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) long-awaited stock market debut may be just weeks away.

The artificial intelligence startup publicly filed its S-1 paperwork for its initial public offering — the prospectus a company must file with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) before selling stock to the public. That started a countdown that could end in one of the largest IPOs in history.

The company hasn't announced a date for its first day of trading, but it's aiming to debut as soon as the week of Nov. 16, according to reports from the Wall Street Journal and Reuters.

Before Anthropic's stock can begin trading, Anthropic's executives and its underwriters have to complete an investor roadshow , set a price, and receive a final green light from regulators.

Earliest date price can be set: Nov. 13, 2026

Exchange : Nasdaq Global Select Market (Class A)

Anthropic reveals amended S-1 outlining huge spending commitments, rising sales

When is the Anthropic IPO? The stock could start trading as soon as Nov. 16.

5 unexpected risk factors Anthropic is worried about

Under SEC rules, the earliest Anthropic could start trading is Monday, Nov. 16, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. Based on the timeline set by SpaceX ( SPCX ) in June that went from public filing to first trade in 23 days, Anthropic would debut on Wednesday, Nov. 18.

Companies that let the SEC review a draft of their IPO paperwork in private are required to wait at least 15 calendar days after making it public before starting their formal roadshow — the meetings where bankers pitch the stock to big investors and take orders. Since Anthropic released its filing to the public on Oct. 26, its roadshow can begin as soon as Nov. 10.

After that, the fastest path runs into a holiday. The SEC is closed for Veterans Day on Nov. 11, and its rules require two business days' notice before the agency declares a filing effective. That makes Friday, Nov. 13, the earliest Anthropic could set its price — a day bankers rarely use, since the stock wouldn't start trading until Monday, leaving buyers to wait out the weekend.

SpaceX started its roadshow the first day it could and priced its stock a week later.

The maker of Claude has yet to disclose how many shares it plans to sell or the price range for its offering.

Those details typically appear in an updated filing before the roadshow begins. The final price is usually set after investors have indicated their demand, the night before the stock starts trading.

Many factors. Market volatility, particularly in comparable stocks already trading, and any outstanding regulatory issues could shift the timetable. The company also hasn't said how long its roadshow will last.

articles.title: OpenAI is quietly renaming data centers ‘compute campuses’
articles.summary: Critics say OpenAI should tackle people’s concerns about data centers, not rebrand them.
articles.body: People hate data centers. They’re loud, resource-hungry eyesores that are so profoundly unpopular they have managed to achieve the near-impossible in today’s polarized political landscape: genuine bipartisan opposition. But what about “compute campuses”? Those sound lovely, right? OpenAI seems to be gambling that a quiet rebrand could be all it takes to defuse the growing political backlash that threatens to derail the infrastructure fueling the AI boom. OpenAI debuted the new terminology on Monday in an announcement launching its new “Grid Protectors Program.” The initiative, starting with an upcoming site in Effingham County, Georgia, aims to address concerns about the strain its sprawling AI infrastructure places on local power grids, particularly during extreme weather and emergencies. It’s a familiar data center problem. Yet in the roughly 900-word announcement, the term “data center” appeared just twice, outnumbered by “compute campus.” The initiative addresses worries about electricity use and the prospect of consumers being left to foot the bill for the AI buildout. OpenAI promises to “pay the costs we create” and “help communities keep the lights on.” Its two mentions of “data center” reinforce the connection: One references US data center capacity and electricity consumption, while the other directly compares OpenAI’s new “compute facilities” with “data centers built even a few years ago.” They’re “much different,” OpenAI says, with the new campuses allowing the company to be rather vaguely “flexible in our power demand.” The terminology appears to be new for OpenAI. A quick search of its website turned up no previous uses of the term. The timing is noteworthy, too. On Monday, Axios reported that OpenAI was planning to rebrand data centers as “AI compute campuses” as part of a policy and PR push after Tuesday’s midterms, anticipating a more hostile regulatory environment if Democrats make gains. Apparently, the rebrand couldn’t wait. Critics, however, aren’t buying it. A new name does nothing to lessen data centers’ environmental footprint, ease the burdens they place on local resources, or address the concerns of nearby residents. Activist groups who spoke to The Verge see the rebrand as a fairly transparent attempt to break free from an increasingly toxic label without meaningfully tackling what made it toxic to begin with. It fits within a broader lobbying push by Big Tech to counter souring public sentiment. “OpenAI is clearly responding to the unpopularity of data centers,” said Holly Elmore, founder and executive director of PauseAI US, a grassroots group campaigning to pause AI development. “Rebranding them ‘compute campuses’ may fool listeners once or twice but it’s not the name ‘data center’ that is unpopular — it’s the giant, polluting construction projects that apparently threatened to turn off people’s heat in the winter,” Elmore told The Verge in an email, calling OpenAI’s electricity announcement “woefully tone deaf.” “Communities that despise them will not be fooled into thinking they have transformed into something else.” Abre’ Conner, director of the NAACP’s Center for Environmental and Climate Justice, was similarly unimpressed. “This feels like an empty solution to an existing issue, which is that the data center infrastructure causes real harm,” she told The Verge. “Changing the name does not fix the problem and makes it seem like people’s health and our environment are public relations problems not environmental and climate concerns.” Conner argued that OpenAI should focus on changing its practices rather than what it calls data centers. “At a time when companies could utilize their resources to develop new models, create more transparency, and slow the infrastructure development, their solution is to just change their name.” Elmore agreed, suggesting the data center rebrand was an attempt by OpenAI to keep up with its rival Anthropic, but that it isn’t “spinning it nearly as well.” Earlier this year, Anthropic pledged to cover 100 percent of the upgrades needed to connect its data centers to power grids, including those that would normally be passed on to consumers. The company has also promised to invest billions of dollars in community projects developed with local leaders, protect local water supplies, and refrain from asking public officials to sign NDAs — a practice that has recently come under scrutiny. Anthropic said those commitments apply to both leased and owned data centers. Leased facilities currently make up most of its infrastructure, though its recent S-1 filing ahead of its IPO indicates the company wants to aggressively build its own, too, with many relying on gas. OpenAI did not respond to The Verge’s request for comment about its decision to change nomenclature, its motivations for doing so, or whether doing so is an attempt to distance itself from the growing controversy surrounding data centers.

articles.title: Apple is all in on AI — its own and everyone else’s
articles.summary: AI was mentioned 45 times on the quarterly earnings call.
articles.body: Apple’s latest earnings show how it’s continuing to capitalize on the AI boom without busting its budget on the infrastructure spending consuming its competitors. Overall, Apple posted its best-ever fiscal year for revenue and earnings per share. iPhone and Mac sales continued to grow strongly in the fourth quarter. iPhone revenue rose 17.5% from a year earlier to a September quarter record of $57.6 billion while Mac revenue climbed 24% to $10.8 billion, its highest level in four years. Shares nevertheless fell in premarket trading Tuesday after Apple warned that rising memory costs would squeeze its profit margins in the holiday quarter. Apple hasn’t disclosed how much of its revenue growth reflects AI demand or higher prices, but its executives clearly see the technology as a way to drive further sales. During the earnings call, CFO Kevan Parekh cited a “wide range of ways that AI can contribute to revenue growth over time.” “On the product side, we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities,” he said. “And we also feel there’s opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities.” Apple can sell its giant user base the devices they use for AI, even if the AI itself comes from someone else. It can collect fees on subscriptions to AI apps. And it can charge customers who want more access to its own AI features. “We see tremendous opportunity in AI,” John Ternus said on his first earnings call as CEO. AI and Apple Intelligence were mentioned a record 45 times on the earnings call, according to financial research platform AlphaSense — even more than on the call following Apple’s unveiling of the technology and plans for a revamped Siri in June 2024. Mentions of AI or “Apple Intelligence” on earnings calls On the call, Apple continued to position itself as the interface through which consumers use AI — including competitors’ technology. With more than 2.5 billion active devices, it already has an enormous audience for whatever AI services emerge. Apple, unlike its Big Tech peers, isn’t pouring comparable sums into infrastructure. Its approach combines on-device processing, its own servers, and outside AI technology. Siri AI uses models developed with Google’s Gemini technology while Apple reportedly plans to let users choose among outside AI providers for features such as writing tools and image generation. Apple spent $2.2 billion on capital expenditures last quarter, compared with Amazon’s $77.3 billion and Alphabet’s $51.4 billion. Those totals cover companywide CapEx, not just AI, and exclude some AI expenses. Apple’s operating expenses rose 21% to $19.2 billion as it increased R&D spending, including on AI. Siri AI’s cloud costs will appear in services cost of sales. Those costs could grow with usage: Parekh said it’s too early to predict how many requests will require servers rather than on-device processing. Still, Apple’s capital spending remains just a fraction of its peers’. More AI usage also gives Apple something to sell. Siri AI is only beginning to reach customers. Apple launched the revamped assistant in beta for US English users in September and expanded it to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October. Apple plans to turn some of that usage into subscription revenue. Ternus said features relying on server-side models, including Siri AI and intelligent photo editing, will have usage limits. Customers who need more capacity “will be able to purchase expanded access in the future,” he said. “In the beginning, iCloud tiers were largely about storage, but we’ve been adding more capabilities and features to it.” Apple also benefits when customers buy its hardware to run AI locally, including models developed by other companies. Mac, Ternus said, is “having an AI moment all its own.” Apple offered specific examples of companies putting its computers to work on AI. Gap is running AI entirely on Mac Mini computers for loss prevention across hundreds of stores, avoiding cloud token costs for those tasks. Christie’s is running local models on Mac Studio computers to improve workflows including pricing estimates. For those customers, buying Apple hardware provides a way to use AI without paying a cloud provider for every request. Mac Mini and Mac Studio, Ternus said, “are pushing the boundaries of local, private AI, giving users the ability to do things once considered impossible.” The Mac Mini’s emergence as an AI machine has given the small, screenless desktop a new constituency among developers and hobbyists looking for a relatively affordable way to run models locally. Earlier this year, then-CEO Tim Cook said customer recognition of the Mac Mini and Mac Studio’s capabilities for AI and agentic tools was happening faster than Apple had predicted, leading to higher-than-expected demand. Apple also makes money when customers subscribe to someone else’s AI. Earlier this year, The Wall Street Journal reported that Apple was on pace to bring in more than $1 billion in App Store fees from generative AI apps in 2026, according to analytics firm AppMagic. That revenue, of course, depends on customers paying through Apple’s system. OpenAI has begun directing potential subscribers to pay through its website instead of the App Store, bypassing Apple’s commissions, The Wall Street Journal reported. Apple’s position gives it a way to profit from competitors’ AI, but those competitors have an incentive to find a route around its fees. Still, Apple already has multiple ways to benefit from people using AI. It can sell the computer, collect a subscription commission, and eventually charge for more of its own services. It doesn’t have to build every model — or fund infrastructure on its competitors’ scale — to get paid.

articles.title: Anthropic employee wages are now costing the AI giant over $100,000 per person per month
articles.summary: Anthropic has already spent nearly $5 billion on personnel in the first nine months of 2026 as revenue soars.
articles.body:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

Anthropic workers are likely making a good salary, plus stock-based compensation

Revenue per employee is more than 2x Meta's and 2.6x Google's

The company is targeting a valuation of around $1.5 trillion

Anthropic has confirmed in a recent S-1 filing that it spent $1.711 billion on personnel in its most recent three-month period, down slightly on the previous quarter's $1.857 billion but up around 3.5x compared with the same quarter in 2025 ($489 million).

With around 5,300 people on the books, it means the average worker set the company back over $322,000 for the quarter, or over $107,000 per month.

While these figures are likely wild overestimates for the average worker's pay, they show just how much the AI giant is having to spend on talent compared with last year.

Anthropic is spending billions on workers' salaries

Crucially, the average worker did not receive $107,000 in a single month, because these figures also include bonuses, employee benefits, payroll taxes and stock-based compensation. An estimated $1.1 billion of the quarterly total came from stock-based compensation, accounting for nearly two-thirds of the total sum.

Still, personnel costs accounted for around 15% of the company's revenue over the first nine months of 2026, which puts Anthropic in a positive position. The company spent $4.8 billion on personnel in the first three quarters.

Flip those figures around and we have a company that's making an estimated $6.6 million in revenue per employee, compared with $3.2 million at Meta and $2.5 million at Google, per Business Insider calculations.

Anthropic doesn't publish salary information, but given its huge expenditure relative to the number of employees, it's clear that recruiting AI talent is expensive. With stock-based compensation accounting for two-thirds of Anthropic's personnel expenditure, workers are likely being attracted by the potential of huge future wealth, rather than immediate compensation.

An upcoming IPO has Anthropic valued at somewhere around the $1.5 trillion mark, per recent Reuters reporting. That would put it ahead of OpenAI, which is now likely targeting a $1.25 trillion valuation, per a separate Reuters report.

articles.title: Google will let schools disable its AI tools, but not without sacrificing Search | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Schools choosing to restrict AI altogether will no longer be able to access Google Search, as AI features are now integrated into the search engine.
articles.body:
Google announced on Tuesday that it plans to disable AI tools for K-12 students next year unless school administrators explicitly turn them on. The tech giant says the change follows consultations with schools, teachers, leading researchers, and policymakers. As a result, Google is revising its approach across Gemini, NotebookLM, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search.

The decision means that schools choosing to restrict AI altogether will no longer be able to access Google Search, as AI features are now integrated into the search engine.

Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times that “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” which means that if a school chooses to restrict AI altogether, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

The change raises an issue for schools. Although teachers may not want students to use AI Overviews in Google Search to conduct research or complete assignments, they likely still want them to be able to have access to the search engine to find sources and other learning materials.

However, Google Search and its AI features are now inseparable. Given the dominance of Google’s suite of apps in classrooms and the widespread use of Chromebooks, the decision underscores the company’s influence over the education sector. Schools that want to continue to have access to Google Search will have to accept its AI features.

“We’ll share more specifics with schools in the coming months ahead of the changes rolling out so they have time to prepare and enable a smooth transition,” Phillips wrote in a blog post . “Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit.”

Google announced the upcoming change alongside the launch of Guided Learning in schools. The tool, which was unveiled earlier this year, sort of functions like an AI tutor, as it’s designed to help users build a deep understanding instead of just getting answers. The launch comes amid concerns that AI chatbots undermine the learning process because they spit out direct answers.

articles.title: AI-related layoffs carry a hidden cost for workers
articles.summary: AI may be repeating a painful pattern from previous technological revolutions: Workers who lose their jobs because of the technology struggle to find employm...
articles.body:
AI may be repeating a painful pattern from previous technological revolutions: Workers who lose their jobs because of the technology struggle to find employment and risk displacement all over again.

Why it matters: AI does not need to trigger mass layoffs to cause lasting damage.

Against the "low-hire, low-fire" backdrop, workers whose skills become obsolete could struggle to find new jobs and suffer years of lost earnings — even if the broader economy avoids a major rise in unemployment.

What they're saying: Workers displaced by earlier technological shifts — including personal computers and industrial automation — often ended up in less-skilled jobs as demand for their expertise faded, Goldman Sachs economist Pierfrancesco Mei wrote in a new note.

"We see early signs of a similar pattern today," Mei wrote.

By the numbers: Workers most likely displaced by AI in 2025 took roughly a month longer to find new employment than other laid-off workers, according to Mei's analysis of more than 15,000 workers who lost jobs between 2016 and 2025.

There's no definitive count of how many workers have lost jobs to AI. The research instead estimates which layoffs were most likely AI-related — based on workers' occupations, industry AI adoption rates and the circumstances, such as whether their positions were eliminated.

Those workers were roughly 10 percentage points more likely to remain unemployed a year after losing their jobs.

Among displaced workers from AI-exposed jobs who found new work in 2025, roughly three-quarters landed in occupations with similar or greater AI exposure — up from just over half in 2023.

The big picture: AI could eventually create new kinds of jobs, but those opportunities may take years to materialize.

Between the lines: Older workers are especially vulnerable to AI-related employment disruption.

Then. A Goldman Sachs analysis from earlier this year, looking at three decades of job losses, found that workers over age 55 displaced from declining occupations suffered earnings losses exceeding 10% when they found new full-time work. Those under 35 saw almost no losses.

Now. Workers under 35 most likely displaced by AI took about three weeks longer to find full-time jobs than other laid-off workers their age. For those 35 and older, that gap was five weeks.

What to watch: Young college graduates are struggling to get hired, raising the possibility that AI is replacing some of the entry-level work that once launched their careers.

Recent graduates' unemployment rate averaged 5.4% in the third quarter, compared with 4% for all workers, according to Federal Reserve Bank of New York data updated Monday. That gap has roughly doubled since 2019.

Underemployment is also rising: About 42% of employed recent graduates held jobs that don't require a degree, up a percentage point from before the pandemic.

The bottom line: Technological revolutions have made the economy more prosperous but left some workers permanently worse off. AI risks repeating that pattern.

articles.summary: Google is disabling Search in schools that choose not to use its AI features. The company says it will turn Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search “entirely off” unless administrators turn them on.
articles.body: Google is completely turning off Search in schools that reject its AI features, the company told The New York Times. The decision was also shared in a broader education-related update from Google on Tuesday, saying that access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search “will be entirely off” for K-12 student accounts unless “administrators explicitly turn them on.” Administrators will not be given the option to toggle Gemini-powered features off without disabling Search, however. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the NYT, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” adding that schools that disable Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.” Google didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment. The announcement comes just months after Google turned its Gemini AI assistant on by default inside the Google Classroom app, which is used by more than 150 million teachers and students globally. The move added to skepticism surrounding Google’s introduction of AI in schools amid reports of declining test scores and other impacts on students’ learning abilities. Last month, lawmakers pressed Google on the “potential harms” of putting its AI products in schools. Although Google is no longer turning on AI features in schools by default, this choice comes at a cost. Several lawmakers and local leaders have responded to Google’s move to block Search, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (D-VT) calling it “extortion” and NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani saying, “no corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.” Rohit Chopra, California’s Secretary of Business & Consumer Services, wrote that Big Tech shouldn’t be able to “strong-arm schools.” Google argues that this change will “give schools more choice, not less,” adding that schools can choose to turn off each service on or off individually. articles.title: Anthropic is still grappling with the economics of compute | TechCrunch
articles.summary: At a moment when Anthropic's compute margins should be getting better, they’re getting worse.
articles.body:
There’s a lot of mystery around the finances of major AI labs, and as Anthropic inches towards it IPO, we’re starting to get some answers. In particular, the company is finally disclosing more about the economics of compute, and how much of Anthropic’s skyrocketing revenue is being lost to compute costs.

In a new filing on Monday , Anthropic released data that showed those margins on compute actually getting worse. The filing was an update to the S-1 released last week — but where that filing’s financial disclosures only covered through June 30 of this year, the new data extended to disclose results through an extra quarter, to September 30. Broadly, Anthropic had a good quarter: revenue reached $17 billion, up from $11.5 billion in the previous quarter, suggesting durable growth. But the operating loss grew at the same time, thanks in large part to growing compute costs.

Looking at the compute margins makes the picture even worse. In the new quarter, compute took up 58% of the company’s revenue, up from 48% the quarter before. At a moment when the company could win over IPO investors by showing margins improving, they’re getting worse.

A chart in the filing shows this even more clearly, tracking the company’s revenue for every dollar spent on compute. Since the start of 2025, it’s been steadily growing, peaking at just over 2x this past quarter, then falling back down to 1.72x.

Many indications imply that this shift in compute margins is more of a blip than a long-term problem, but it still tells us important things about the business of running a major lab. Trying to keep up with demand, Anthropic’s compute bill shot up to $10 billion for the quarter, including, as the filing notes, “$5.0 billion of compute under short-term commitments, which currently costs significantly more than comparable compute procured under our multi-year commitments.” Basically, demand was growing so fast that Anthropic had to scramble for compute, which meant paying higher rates.

Some of those deals have already played out in public. Anthropic has been paying SpaceX $1.25 billion a month for compute, alongside multibillion-dollar deals with Nscale , Akamai , and Volta . In the parlance of the industry, these are neoclouds rather than hyperscalers — smaller outfits that offer more flexible compute deals at higher rates.

Anthropic’s margins got worse in Q3 because of deals like these, and there’s no sign they’ll be able to do without them anytime soon. As the new filing puts it, “We expect compute and infrastructure expenses to increase in absolute dollars and remain our largest operating expense for the foreseeable future as additional committed compute becomes available to us under multi-year arrangements with CSPs, and as we continue to invest in additional compute.”

Anthropic is still trying to lower its compute costs. In particular, the company talks quite a bit about its efforts to build its own compute base under a project it calls “Anthropic Direct.” But with demand growing so fast, those efforts aren’t going to be able to keep pace, and the neoclouds will continue to be the best option they have.

In a sense, these are champagne problems. As long as revenue is growing at nearly 50% a quarter, few investors will worry about high compute costs — and the moment demand slows down, investors may be comforted by a compute picture that has gotten a lot sunnier. But it’s a reminder of how much AI labs still depend on the trillion-dollar infrastructure buildout — and how vulnerable they are to hiccups in that process. It’s easy to imagine the data center buildout slowing down over the next year if bond markets get skittish or local opposition gets more intense. There’s not much Anthropic can do to address either of those risks, and either one would make a messy compute picture a whole lot messier.

In the meantime, the future of Anthropic and other labs will be at the mercy of compute prices.

articles.title: OpenAI says ChatGPT is catching up to Google in search
articles.summary: ChatGPT processes one-fifth the volume of search queries as Google, per OpenAI.
articles.body: In many circles, “Ask Chat” has replaced “Google it,” and that’s reflected in a new announcement from OpenAI: the volume of search queries run through ChatGPT now equals 20 percent of the volume run through Google. Adam Fry, OpenAI’s consumer product lead for ChatGPT, made the announcement at a press event on Monday. He said the company defines a search as any time a user inputs a query that results in a web search, as opposed to tasks like defining a term or a simple how-to explanation. (Fry did not specify the source of the Google search volume number.) Having one-fifth as many searches as Google is still a long way from overtaking it, but for comparison, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said during Google’s 2023 antitrust trial that Bing had about 3 percent of the search engine market share after trying for more than a decade. During the trial, Google described AI as a potential disruptor, arguing ChatGPT was poised to seriously compete with it — now, OpenAI seems to agree. (OpenAI likely uses Microsoft Bing for a significant part of its searches, along with its in-house search index, although there is still some speculation that it routes some queries through Google.) The news comes amid an ongoing search engine shake-up, as Google continues to reduce conventional referrals to third-party sites and invests heavily in AI tools — not just AI Overview but also additional generative AI capabilities, including personalized search results with visualizations and charts. But as search queries increasingly route through OpenAI and other AI labs’ services, other companies are investing in the same types of AI-focused search experience, even if they call it something else: for OpenAI, it’s “Intelligent UI,” or creating a visual and interactive interface within a chatbot response. “That’s where the future of this technology goes. You’re talking to a canvas,” Fry said. Much like Google, OpenAI sees a potential path to profitability through ads, particularly as it approaches an IPO potentially slated for early next year. OpenAI has defended its ads in the past, and Fry told reporters they hadn’t produced a lasting backlash. “Ads have not negatively impacted the product or the usage of the product,” he said, adding that “most people do not seem to mind ads in the product.” OpenAI announced last month that the company would begin introducing images of sponsored products and services in ChatGPT rather than just a company’s name, logo, and a link to its product like before. “Ads have maybe shown us that we could be doing this more, actually,” Fry said.

articles.title: Reddit tests ads in search results as traffic declines and growth concerns mount | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The new ad placements could help Reddit squeeze more revenue from existing users as Google's AI search changes how people discover its content.
articles.body:
Just days after warning investors about declining search traffic and a weaker-than-expected revenue forecast, Reddit is looking for more ways to make money from its existing users. On Tuesday, the company announced that it’s beginning to test ad placements in its search results pages, allowing advertisers to reach users as they search for products, recommendations, and other information on its platform.

“Ads in search may appear based on a range of factors, including contextual relevance to a user’s search query,” Reddit shared in its announcement about the new ad placements. “This is an initial test with a select group of eligible advertisers. During this test, we will evaluate and understand how users respond to these ads so we can refine the experience for users and advertisers over time.”

The company offered examples of what sort of ads might appear, suggesting that a search for “espresso station” might display ads for espresso machines, coffee, or mugs, while a search for “home office setup” could surface ads for things like monitors, desks, and office chairs.

The ad test comes at a time when Reddit is reckoning with how AI has been changing the web’s landscape, and subsequently its reach.

Despite beating Wall Street’s estimates for revenue and earnings per share, the company’s stock dropped after it reported its third-quarter results last week , with fourth-quarter guidance that predicted sales of $1 billion to $1.03 billion, below expectations of $1.05 billion. This was tied to Reddit’s declining search traffic referrals resulting from Google’s move to an AI-powered search experience. AI search now sends less traffic to publishers’ websites, as features like AI Mode provide answers directly on Google’s Search Result pages, reducing clicks to other websites.

Reddit also said that its global daily active users were flat quarter-over-quarter in Q3, reaching 130.3 million, while U.S. daily active users dropped from 53.2 million in Q2 to 50.7 million in the quarter, and were down 2% year-over-year. The company noted that if the trend continues, daily active users could decline to a low double-digit percentage by the fourth quarter.

This leaves the company needing to earn more revenue from its existing users, which is where these new ads come in. The ads could prove to be more valuable to Reddit after it makes its planned shift to a logged-in experience, which was also announced during earnings. The company said it will make the transition gradually, initially in markets outside the U.S.

The decision to limit its content to logged-in users serves multiple purposes — it protects Reddit’s site from unauthorized AI scraping, and it increases its value to advertisers. Logged-in users are worth more to advertisers because they provide additional signals about their interests and behavior, allowing for better-targeted, more profitable ads.

articles.title: Google Lets Schools Turn Off Gemini, But Not the AI in Search
articles.summary: Schools that want their K-12 students to have access to Google Search will soon have to turn it on themselves, and the AI features built into Search will com...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Schools that want their K-12 students to have access to Google Search will soon have to turn it on themselves, and the AI features built into Search will come with it, under changes the Alphabet Inc. company announced Tuesday.

Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post that Search, along with Google's Gemini chatbot, Gemini Notebook and Gemini in Google Classroom, will be set off by default for K-12 student accounts until school administrators turn them on. Search, however, will include AI features. The company said it would share more specifics with schools "in the coming months" ahead of the rollout and that the decision followed conversations with schools, teachers, researchers and policymakers.

The change comes as Google, whose Chromebooks are the most widely used laptops in American classrooms, faces growing resistance to AI from parents and school districts. In August, Google turned on its chatbot by default in Google Classroom for schools that already let students use Gemini, drawing criticism from school leaders.

In early September, the country's two largest school systems pulled back on AI. New York City barred students through eighth grade from using generative AI this school year, and Los Angeles Unified blocked students from generative AI on district-issued devices, including standalone tools and AI features built into Google Workspace apps.

Under Google's new controls, such school districts would have to choose between giving students Google Search with its AI features embedded or no Google Search at all.

The company also said Guided Learning, a study mode Google first released in its Gemini app, would be extended into Search. When Google's systems detect a student is looking for certain types of homework help, Search will walk them through a problem one step at a time. A student who pastes in a physics problem or asks for help with a book report, for example, will get prompts meant to make them work through the concepts instead of skipping to the answer.

Google will pilot Guided Learning within Google Search in select US schools later this month and plans to expand it to other districts after collecting feedback from teachers. The company said its research showed the feature led to "measurable learning gains for students," though the blog post didn't cite independent evaluations.

articles.title: Google to schools: Keep our AI turned on, or lose access to Search
articles.summary: Google says it's giving schools more control over what AI tools students can use, but they'll lose access to Search if they turn AI off entirely.
articles.body:
Google is making it easier for K-12 schools that use its products to control what AI tools kids can access. However, if schools opt to turn off AI entirely, they'll lose access to Google Search. The company announced the changes in a post on its education blog , where it also unveiled a new AI tool to help guide student learning in Google Search.

"Search and A.I. are deeply integrated," said Chris Phillips, Google's vice president for education, in a statement to The New York Times . He added that, if a school bans AI, students "will not have access to search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available."

Recently, parents and some educators have been vocal about pushing back against AI in classrooms. In September, both New York and Los Angeles announced plans to restrict access to AI tools on school devices. Google says its updated policies aim to give schools more control over students' AI use — but removing access to Google Search if schools turn off AI entirely may put administrators in a bind.

The move reflects Google's priorities in recent years as it has sought to integrate AI across its products. The most visible manifestation is in Google Search, where the company's AI Overviews appear at the top of most search results now, pulling information to ostensibly help answer questions directly on the search results page.

The company is eager to bring some of those same AI capabilities to classrooms. "We believe AI products should support 'productive struggle' — enabling students to be actively challenged without getting so overwhelmed that they give up. That's the philosophy behind Guided Learning," Google said in its blog post, referring to the tool it's bringing to Search and Google Classroom in schools.

In a statement to The New York Times, Lina Khan, the former chair of the Federal Trade Commission under the Biden administration, said Google is using its position to "coerce schools" into using AI. "As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don't fall in line."

In a post on X posted later on Tuesday, Google sought to clarify its plans. "We want to clarify what we announced today about our education services. Today's announcements give schools more choice, not less." The company added that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search will be off by default. Schools can then choose to turn on "one, two, or all of these services individually."

articles.title: Data centers are turning to old jet engines as the wait for power grows | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The years-long wait for access to the grid and new turbines is causing data center builders to turn to an unusual, less-efficient and less environmentally friendly solution: once-discarded jet engines.
articles.body:
Stuck in years-long lines for grid connections and new turbines, some AI data centers are making their own electricity with converted jet engines, the New York Times reported Tuesday.

The engines, pulled from retired aircraft and rebuilt to burn natural gas, aren’t anyone’s idea of a permanent power plant. But they’re another sign of how far power supply has fallen behind the AI buildout.

For companies stuck in those lines, the main draw of converted jet engines is how quickly the engines can be up and running. “It’s all about getting power as fast as possible,” Rystad Energy analyst Audun Martinsen told the Times. With jet-powered units, “they can have a data center running in 24 months,” he said.

Hooking up 100 megawatts to the grid in Northern Virginia, by comparison, takes about seven years , according to the International Energy Agency. Most power capacity is expected to come on by 2031, an executive at Mitsubishi Power, one of the world’s top makers of power generation equipment, told Bloomberg last week .

In some cases, these delays are already costing some data center operators business. Last month, Microsoft pulled out as the anchor customer for Nscale’s data center in Loughton, England, after the local utility said it couldn’t deliver enough power until the early to mid-2030s.

Elon Musk’s xAI is among the companies already using the engines, having installed eight converted jet-engine turbines in Mississippi to help power its Colossus 2 data center in Memphis, the Times reported, citing state permits and satellite imagery. The units come from ProEnergy, which rebuilds a GE engine commonly found on Boeing jets.

In 2025, OpenAI followed Musk’s lead with gas turbines at its first Stargate site in Abilene, Texas. Crusoe, a Denver-based startup that builds AI data centers, is constructing that Abilene campus and ordered 13 of ProEnergy’s converted units in April.

In September, Crusoe walked away from a $1.25 billion deal to buy 29 natural gas turbines from Boom Supersonic, a startup developing a supersonic passenger jet that has also begun selling a version of that jet’s engine as a power plant for data centers. A Crusoe spokesperson told TechCrunch at the time that the company still plans to use turbines.

Currently the Trump administration is adding to the pressure by encouraging data centers to generate their own electricity.

Converted jet engines come with trade-offs, though: They’re less efficient and pollute more than turbines designed for conventional gas plants, and it takes more of them to make the same amount of power, according to the Times. That may ultimately make converted jet engines a short-term play with some experts saying that efficiency and environmental concerns may grow in importance in a year or two.

articles.title: Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models' identity | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Called FlashProve, the system would let anyone check that an AI response really came from the model it claims to be from.
articles.body:
Anthropic is working on an open source system to verify which AI model produced a given output, according to a blog post published Tuesday. The system, called FlashProve , is built to provide what researchers call “provable inference” — a cryptographic proof, essentially a mathematical guarantee, that a given output came from a specific model. It’s meant to let users confirm that the answer they received really came from the model they think they’re using.

Similar to cryptographic email signatures that let recipients confirm a message really came from its claimed sender, FlashProve would be robust against impostors attempting to disguise one model as another, even when the impostor is the lab that built and runs the model. In particular, the researchers note that the system could be used to prevent an AI company from secretly swapping in a cheaper model to cut costs, or a more expensive model to inflate its performance results.

FlashProve could also be used to verify claims by third parties that a specific task was done by an advanced model. “A developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model,” the researchers write. “How can a user verify these claims?”

To work, the system requires AI labs to publish a “fingerprint” of each model they release that can later be matched to specific outputs and verified cryptographically. Crucially, the fingerprints don’t reveal a model’s weights, the internal numbers that define how it behaves and which closed-model makers like Anthropic and OpenAI keep private. That means labs could publish the fingerprints without giving up their most valuable asset, enabling the system to work with commercial models, too. The system is also designed to be lightweight, so verification could be performed on a local device.

As part of the announcement, researchers released a detailed technical specification and working code for various elements of the system, which is publicly available under an open source license on GitHub . Research in the system is ongoing, and there are no plans to deploy it at Anthropic or any other lab.

“This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda,” researchers explain in the announcement post. “We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.”

articles.title: Please stop asking me when the AI bubble will pop
articles.summary: The bond offerings keep coming, even as some of the most influential people in the bond market, such as the CEO of PIMCO, warn about an AI downturn.
articles.body: People, including on this staff, keep asking me with varying degrees of excitement or trepidation when the AI bubble will burst. I’ll tell you what I tell them: If I knew that, I would make a life-changing bet on the market, levered up as far as I could, and then, after I made my money, go retire on a beach somewhere. Maybe run a cat sanctuary, who knows. What I can tell you is that I read with interest a story in Bloomberg this morning: “Wall Street CEOs, Big Money Managers Divided Over AI Risks.” The story itself is a roundup of stuff said at the 2026 Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit in Hong Kong. Here’s what caught my attention: The CEO of Pacific Investment Management Co. — that’s PIMCO, the legendary bond firm — told listeners that there’s going to be a downturn in the AI market “and then things are going to break.” The astronomically expensive AI buildout has swamped debt markets — making it harder to raise cash. But there’s still more debt coming, and people still want to buy it. For instance, Meta drew $58 billion in orders for a bond offering that’s expected to be $15 billion to $20 billion, Bloomberg reported today. Oracle said Monday it would need another $20 billion in bonds, on top of its existing steep commitments. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, is selling €6 billion (or about $6.7 billion) of bonds. Even Microsoft recently sold bonds, for the first time in a decade — $25 billion of them. The PIMCO CEO — his name is Emmanuel Roman, but his job is what matters here — has estimated that the AI buildout could create $2 trillion in financing needs over the next five years. The entire total US bond market is about $12 trillion. I am harping on PIMCO because it has been instrumental in the AI trade. It was among the group of financiers that did the first CoreWeave chip-based financing in 2023. It made a quick $2 billion in paper gains from $29 billion in Meta bonds, meant to support the AI buildout, last year. It bought $4 billion of SpaceX bonds last month. If PIMCO’s CEO is publicly sounding the alarm about a bubble popping, that’s a big deal — especially since the company just sold a bunch of its AI debt. It’s not just PIMCO urging caution. Apollo Global Management, which lately had been talking with SpaceX about a $40 billion chip deal, is also warning of AI risk. Apollo president Jim Zelter told analysts today that while he expects society will use “dramatically more computing power in the future” and that AI is improving quickly, there is still significant uncertainty. “What we don’t know is how pricing and economics will evolve.” The sheer volume of interest on Meta’s bonds suggests we are not at the top of the market. But there have been reports from China that its AI bubble burst some time ago. Meanwhile Wall Street banks were tripping over themselves to finance $63 billion in debt from Anthropic — not even a hyperscaler. This is what I mean when I say “I don’t know.” I do think, though, that something major — PIMCO’s Roman singled out US rate hikes, war, or a eurozone crisis as potential triggers — could flip this market. We’re not in go-go-go territory now. Maybe that will change; it’s possible Anthropic’s IPO will go blockbuster and it’ll be like when someone rolls up to a party that’s running low on beer with a 24-pack. But as more people are expressing caution — and particularly after the disaster at Situational Awareness — the best part of the party might be over.

articles.body: Former OpenAI employees say they were not surprised after the company discovered a hidden audio recording device in an executive conference room in October, as they had raised concerns about its internal security practices for years. According to a Reuters report, some employees warned OpenAI's leadership and board that its security controls were too weak and could allow outsiders, including foreign governments, to access sensitive information about its artificial intelligence (AI) technology. The concerns came into focus after FBI announced on October 13 that a Saudi national, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, had been arrested and charged with allegedly placing a hidden recording device in an OpenAI executive conference room. Alfozan was working as an engineer at the company at the time.OpenAI employees had raised security concerns for yearsAccording to five people familiar with the matter cited by Reuters, OpenAI employees raised concerns about the company's security practices even before ChatGPT launched in late 2022. Some employees believed that the company's internal controls were so weak that foreign governments or other outside actors could easily obtain sensitive details about its technology. They also said that employees with access to OpenAI's code could view details of projects that were not directly related to their work.Some staff members reportedly felt that OpenAI's leadership was more focused on keeping up with rivals such as Google and Anthropic than on strengthening security.What did the Saudi national allegedly doAccording to a court filing cited by Reuters, Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly used an AI tool designed for OpenAI employees to search for internal documents about executives travelling to Saudi Arabia. He also reportedly looked for information about which OpenAI officials were likely to attend meetings with Saudi ministers.The filing also stated that Alfozan was in regular contact with a Saudi royal who had tried to recruit him for a new AI venture in Saudi Arabia.OpenAI has started strengthening its security systemsOpenAI has reportedly begun taking steps to address its internal security concerns. Thibault Sottiaux, a senior executive overseeing product development, has recently taken charge of an internal effort to secure the company's systems. In August, Sottiaux reassigned around a quarter of OpenAI's production engineers to work on improving its security infrastructure, according to one person familiar with the matter.The company has also restricted access to sensitive work and said that its most sensitive projects are stored in separate code repositories with strict access controls. OpenAI said its main code repository does not contain all of its code or critical details of its AI models, including model weights, which determine how a model behaves. The company also said it now conducts regular security reviews of its internal tools.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Sam Altman doesn’t want AI deciding what humans do; OpenAI CEO says: People should not be relegated to a role of...
articles.summary: Sam Altman has spent years telling the world that superintelligence is closer than it looks.
articles.body: Sam Altman has spent years telling the world that superintelligence is closer than it looks. Now the OpenAI CEO wants to be clear about one thing: whenever it shows up, it should not be the one running things. In a three-line post on X, Altman said people should always be in control of the future, and that OpenAI is against humans being “relegated to a role of doing things that ‘AI systems think makes sense to reward in humans’.” He saved the sharpest line for the end. People should not cede control of the future to superintelligence, he wrote, “and that requirement should ultimately constrain AI progress.”The words in quotation marks are borrowed, though Altman did not say from whom. What stands out more is the final sentence. The head of the company that set off the AI race with ChatGPT has now put in writing that human control should decide how far and how fast AI goes.Sam Altman believes AI has already overtaken the smartest scientistsThe post did not come out of nowhere. Speaking at a conference in Abu Dhabi earlier this week, Altman made the same case for keeping people in charge, and paired it with a striking claim. At the start of 2026, he said, AI “was mostly not as smart as our smartest scientists. And now it’s mostly smarter than them.”He had sketched out how he wants that power spread around in a podcast conversation with Stripe co-founder John Collison last month. Altman said he would rather see “a trillion AIs of slightly superhuman intelligence join society than one AI of 1 trillion IQ.” Society holds together, he argued, because lots of people keep each other in check, and AI should work the same way.The industry, he added, may need to agree on limits to how smart any single model is allowed to get, possibly for a long time. He also had little patience for a future where people live on a basic income while a small group in “a few square miles of San Francisco make all the decisions about the future.”OpenAI CEO admits keeping superhuman AI in check may not be easyThe same podcast offers a clue to why Altman is pressing the point now. Asked whether AI models can simply be locked inside secure digital sandboxes, he said that approach “works to a point.” Monitoring what the models are doing, including what goes on inside them, can take things further.Beyond that, he said, it comes down to trust. Developers would need to be certain a model is aligned with what its operators want, and that it will “value people being in control of the future.” For a system far smarter than any human expert, Altman was not sure even that would hold. “If you imagine a theoretical AI that is a million times smarter than the smartest security researcher,” he said, “would you really be willing to trust that sandbox?”He also pointed to how quickly AI is getting better at finding software flaws. Now that people have started using models to scan code across the internet, Altman expects the world to discover “many more serious vulnerabilities than we expect.”Altman’s post builds on a position he has been settling into for a few months. When Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on AI companies in September to slow how fast their models improve, Altman’s response was, “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier.” That same month, he went a step further at the UN Security Council, saying AI systems should not be trained unless developers can make a strong case that they will stay under human control.You use AI every day. articles.title: Nvidia China Clients to Get 1% of $70 Billion RTX Chips Ordered
articles.summary: Chinese AI developers expect to receive just a small fraction of the advanced Nvidia Corp. chips they've ordered over the next several months, as the US comp...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Chinese AI developers expect to receive just a small fraction of the advanced Nvidia Corp. ( NVDA ) chips they've ordered over the next several months, as the US company struggles to boost production to meet soaring demand.

Alibaba Group Holding Ltd., Tencent Holdings Ltd., ByteDance Ltd. and other Chinese AI and cloud firms have in total ordered about 6 million of Nvidia's RTX Pro 5500 chips, according to people familiar with the matter. Yet the companies predict they will get only some tens of thousands, or roughly 1%, within the next four months, said the people, asking not to be named discussing a private matter.

At more than $11,000 a chip, the total orders so far are valued at about $70 billion, the people said.

Chinese hyperscalers' strong appetite for the chips underscores the enormous shortage of AI computing power in the country. It also exposes the limitations of local hardware manufacturers despite the technological progress they've been making. Scant chip supply will make it harder for the Chinese AI developers to catch up with the US market leaders.

While the US bars Nvidia from selling its most cutting-edge chips to China, the RTX Pro 5500 isn't quite powerful enough to face such restrictions. Yet in China, it is among the best AI chips available, as local manufacturers Huawei Technologies Co. and Alibaba's T-Head trail the production and technological capabilities of their US rivals.

Nvidia, the global AI hardware leader, has lobbied the US government for years to be able to sell more chips to Chinese customers. Yet with insufficient global production capacity, the US company is prioritizing its most sophisticated and higher-margin semiconductors, used by the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic PBC.

Major Chinese AI developers expect the first batch of several thousand RTX Pro 5500 chips to be delivered by the end of this year, followed by another batch of tens of thousands around February, said the people. Those are the only confirmed shipments so far, one of the people said.

The Chinese hyperscalers estimate they could receive roughly 700,000 RTX Pro 5500 units by the end of 2027, as Nvidia is expected to ramp up production, said one of the people, citing internal calculations of a key buyer. The final shipment sizes could change, depending on Nvidia's capacity adjustments.

articles.title: Google hasn’t figured out how to make AI pay like its search engine
articles.summary: Google says AI is boosting searches, but that activity isn’t translating into faster growth for the business that pays for it.
articles.body: Search queries are growing at their fastest rate in five years, Google parent Alphabet said in its earnings report last week. However, Google’s Search revenue growth slowed to 12 percent year over year in the third quarter, down from roughly 17 percent in the previous quarter. Meanwhile, growth in paid clicks — clicks on ads that generate revenue for Google — slowed from 13 percent to 8 percent. That’s still substantial growth, but not the direction investors were hoping for from a company planning to spend about $200 billion this year on infrastructure, largely to support AI. Alphabet shares have fallen about 14 percent since it reported earnings last week, as investors question the costs and returns of the company’s AI ambitions. Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said currency effects were the biggest driver of the revenue-growth slowdown, alongside changes in spending by advertisers in particular industries. But Google’s AI makeover also contributed to the slowdown: AI Mode queries were growing strongly but monetizing at a lower rate than traditional searches, Schindler says. He added that Google feels good about its trajectory and that its “ad experiments have shown promising results.” It remains unclear whether that reflects a deliberate rollout of ads, as Google says, or a more fundamental problem with advertising in AI search. YOY growth for search revenue vs. paid clicks in Q1-3 in 2026 “This is the first major disruption that Google is facing to its core business in decades,” Nate Elliott, an eMarketer principal analyst covering AI and advertising, tells The Verge. AI is changing how people find information — and whether they click on the ads that fund Google’s business. What Google’s core Search business looks like increasingly depends on what you ask. In many cases, AI Overviews add generated summaries to search results; electing AI Mode turns searching into a conversation. But someone searching for Nikes can still get familiar shopping listings and text ads, says Andy Taylor, vice president of research at digital advertising agency Tinuiti. They’re looking to buy shoes rather than get an AI explanation of them. Google’s argument is that AI is expanding the business. Schindler says most AI Mode queries are “incremental” — additional questions rather than replacements for existing searches. Many are also “upper-funnel,” meaning people are researching potential purchases before they know what they want. The company sees those searches as opportunities to sell more ads over time. Google is currently expanding ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode, including internationally and across multiple turns of US AI Mode conversations. It has also floated bringing ads to its standalone Gemini app, saying formats developed for AI Mode could carry over, but hasn’t announced when. The thing is, Google, as well as competitors like OpenAI, are still figuring out how to make ads work in AI — both delivering results for advertisers and avoiding alienating the people using their AI tools. For now, advertisers are still getting results from Google. Tinuiti’s same-store advertisers increased their Google paid search spending 14 percent year over year in the third quarter while maintaining their return-on-ad-spend targets. “We’re still seeing a good return, and we’re not seeing performance take a hit,” Taylor says. The catch is that advertisers can’t isolate how Google’s AI ads are doing. Google doesn’t let them separately target that inventory or break out its performance, Taylor says. Steady overall returns could mean AI ad traffic is still too small to noticeably affect the results, or that it performs similarly to existing inventory. Taylor suspects it’s mostly the former. That leaves an important question unanswered: How much will AI add to Google’s advertising business, and how much could it replace? Additional queries could bring in new revenue even if each earns less than a traditional search. The risk is that AI Mode also draws people away from searches that Google monetizes more effectively. Google’s claim that most AI Mode queries are additional doesn’t tell us how much revenue it could lose from the searches AI Mode replaces. “If people are clicking through less often,” Elliott says, “that is a challenge that they need to figure out.” The promise of conversational advertising is that people share much more about their needs than they would in a few keywords. But platforms still have to identify which parts of a conversation matter and match them with the right ads. “It’s not a slam dunk that it’s going to turn into more effective advertising,” Elliott says. An early study of ChatGPT ads suggests richer conversations don’t automatically translate into more retail sales. An October working paper found that US visits from ChatGPT ads generated 64 percent less revenue for retailers per session than visits from Google Search ads: $0.89 versus $2.45. The working paper measures retailers’ sales rather than platform revenue, and its findings about ChatGPT don’t establish how Google’s own AI ads perform. Taylor cautions that those comparisons depend on what people are searching for. Someone searching Google for Nike shoes may already be ready to buy, while someone asking an AI tool which running shoes to choose is still researching. A higher sales return could reflect that difference in purchase intent rather than more effective ads. Google’s existing business has given it room to take its time with AI ads, Taylor says. He points to its successful shift to mobile: Early phone traffic was less valuable to advertisers because shopping on a phone was cumbersome, but that changed. Elliott cautions that finding effective ad formats can take years. Search engines started with banner ads before adopting paid listings; social media went through its own experimentation. Today’s formats may not be the ones that ultimately work. But Google’s mounting AI spending raises the stakes. Search revenue is still growing by double digits, but the company has yet to show how well its new way of searching can pay. “They absolutely do not have it all figured out,” Elliott says. “No one has it all figured out.”

articles.title: Sam Altman addresses RAM comments: people should ‘put as much as they want in their computers’
articles.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in posts on X that he wants the world to have more RAM, following comments on the RAM shortage in a Cheeky Pint interview.
articles.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman spent election night defending his position on PC RAM purchases. He changed his name on X to “Ram Altman” in response to another user’s comment, saying, “i actually do want the world to have tons of memory and people to put as much as they want in their computers, and it is fucking annoying that this was taken out of context. i have been arguing for the world to ramp up memory production for a long time.” He replied to another comment, saying, “i want you to have so much ram lets build more.” [Media: [Media: Altman’s posts follow an interview on the Cheeky Pint podcast, where he said “it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used five percent of the time.” AI data centers have been snapping up the world’s RAM supply, driving shortages that are leading to tech price hikes and making it tough for many people to “have so much ram” like Altman says he wants. The RAM shortage might not let up anytime soon, either — Intel’s expecting it to last through at least next year, and SK Hynix predicted it could drag on until 2030.

articles.title: Uber only fulfilled 4 rides from AI agents last quarter
articles.summary: Uber disclosed that third-party AI agents booked only four rides in Q3 2026, downplaying near-term disintermediation risks as the platform bets on direct customer loyalty.
articles.body: AI agents won’t be stealing Uber’s lunch any time soon. Only four rides were arranged by third-party AI agents during the third quarter of 2026, Uber executives disclosed during an earnings call this morning. The volume of Uber Eats orders fulfilled by AI agents was a little higher, with the company recording “around 500” during the week of Halloween, out of a total 320 million Uber rides and Uber Eats deliveries. This is the first time that Uber has disclosed the number of third-party AI agents that have arranged deliveries or rides on its platform. With the rise of AI agents like Meta’s Muse or OpenAI’s Dots, some experts are predicting that platforms like Uber and DoorDash are at risk of disintermediation, in which customers use AI agents to order food or book a ride, rather than visiting the app itself. But in these early days, it seems like the risk is still very small. During the call, Uber’s executives expressed an openness to working with third-party AI companies to make things easier for agents to use their platform — while also expressing confidence that their customers will continue to prefer the experience of using the Uber app directly. “We hope that there will be more traction,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the call. “We do think that we want to make services that are available to consumers in a delightful, easy way. We think our direct services are going to be the most delightful and easy, but we will work with these third parties.” He continued, “It is just very, very early, and we want to make sure we are not dependent on any one player, and I think we are very well positioned in this environment going forward.” As we’ve noted before, this first wave of AI agents still have a long way to go before people begin seeing them as a viable way to order food or book a ride somewhere. There still is a lot of friction points. And platform operators like Uber or DoorDash have little incentive to allow these agents to barge in and replace their own customers. Which is not to say the AI companies won’t inevitably figure it out! These companies know this is one of their primary use cases, and their best path to a more profitable future. But getting Uber to agree to more disintermediation will be a tough ask. Uber is developing its own AI tools that are designed to keep customers using its own platform. Earlier this year, the company rolled out a new Cart Assistant for Uber Eats, in which an AI bot will build a grocery list based on an image of a recipe or a text prompt.

articles.title: AI chatbots are giving medication advice, and some of it is deadly
articles.summary: Our research suggests this is not a one-off problem with one old model.
articles.body:
Last week, the parents of Bowen Wan, a 31-year-old software engineer with epilepsy, sued OpenAI . Their lawsuit says that ChatGPT coached their daughter to taper off her seizure medication without a doctor’s supervision and told her to keep the plan from her doctors. She died in February. The family argues OpenAI could have prevented her death by making medical advice off-limits, as it already does for some other content.

OpenAI said it involved an older version of ChatGPT that is no longer available. Our research suggests this is not a one-off problem with one old model.

At Vals AI, an independent artificial intelligence evaluator where I am a clinical researcher, we recently tested how 17 current AI chatbots respond to teenagers. Working with 12 clinicians who treat teens every day, we simulated more than 30,000 conversations between teens and chatbots. Medication came up in more than 5,500 of them.

When it did, chatbots made a medication decision for the teen 22 percent of the time: which medicine to take, how much, or whether to stop or change a prescribed one. Telling the chatbot that it was talking to a teen cut that to 8 percent, but not to zero.

The chatbots varied widely. OpenAI’s newest model and Meta’s Muse Spark almost never did this, while others did in about two out of three cases. And when a teen pushed back after a chatbot refused to advise them, chatbots were more likely to give in: failures rose from 15 percent to 25 percent.

About 1 in 4 U.S. adults now use AI tools for health information, and nearly 1 in 5 U.S. teens and young adults have used AI chatbots for mental health advice. People turn to AI because it is always available and easy to reach. The clinicians we work with say the same. Teenagers tell them they use AI the way adults use Google.

Sometimes that helps. As a researcher at Stanford, one teen I interviewed told me, “If I did not have AI to ask about my symptoms, I probably would have had to go to the ER.” The chatbot had reassured him that his symptoms were likely harmless. And he didn’t get sick. But what if he had?

In some of the conversations we tested, chatbots went further than giving advice. Some told teens that side effects were a reason to stop their medication, and to tell their doctor so. In another case, a chatbot helped a teen persuade their doctor to take them off their medication without telling their parents.

There are important caveats. Our conversations were simulated, and each ran for up to 20 exchanges. Real conversations can stretch across days and many sessions, and our results show that a chatbot’s boundaries can weaken as a conversation goes on, so the real-world risk may be even greater.

The need for regulation and independent evaluation is clear. How to regulate is harder.

Many policies say a chatbot may not pose as a licensed professional. However, a disclaimer that the AI is not a medical provider is not enough. AI sounds human and authoritative, and many people trust its advice. For example, as one teen I interviewed put it, “AI is like a machine that knows more than Google.” Policy must therefore judge what chatbots actually say and do in a conversation, not only the disclaimers they show.

Second, doctors need training on patients’ AI use. Many doctors we talk to do not know that their patients are talking to AI. Medical education needs to accept that many patients have already asked an AI before they ever see a doctor and should teach clinicians to ask about it.

Finally, the public needs to know the risks. Some medical associations have published advice about AI, but few people read it. Public campaigns can reach more people. The Center for Humane Technology, for example, runs a campaign about the dangers of AI replacing human relationships. A similar campaign could warn about AI’s medical advice.

We talk a lot about the long-term, catastrophic risks of AI. But people are being harmed by bad AI medical advice now. Regulation can’t wait.

Dr. Caroline Figueora , MD, Ph.D., a doctor most recently at Stanford University, is a clinical researcher at independent AI evaluation company Vals AI and a Public Voices Fellow on Youth Well-Being and Power with The OpEd Project.

articles.title: Google faces backlash for plan that would turn off Search for schools that restrict AI | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Politicians on the left, like NYC mayor Zohran Mamdani and former FTC chair Lina Khan, accused Google of acting as an unregulated monopoly.
articles.body:
Google was met with swift backlash on Tuesday after it announced that schools using Google’s K-12 software will not be able to use Search unless they opt in to using AI tools.

Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times that “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” so if a student’s school doesn’t opt in to using AI tools like Gemini, then students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

Even as Google made this announcement on a busy Election Day, several left-leaning politicians took time to speak up about their concerns.

Senator Bernie Sanders (I-VT) accused Google in an X post of “extortion,” writing that “Google is threatening schools: if you stop your students from using AI, we will cut off your access to Google Search.” Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) said on X that Google is “more concerned with forcing Gemini into schools than enabling students to succeed.”

Lina Khan, the former FTC chair and staunch advocate against monopolies, also condemned Google’s decision as anti-competitive.

“This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service,” she wrote . “Multiple courts have found Google liable for violating antitrust laws, and this latest move shows it remains unchastened.”

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused Google of being a monopoly, commenting , “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.”

While Search is a necessary tool for information gathering, educators worry that its built-in AI overviews could dissuade students from finding answers themselves. For millions of students required to use Chromebooks and Google education tools, using a different search engine isn’t a simple fix.

Google says that it’s working on a “Guided Learning” tool for student accounts in Search, which is supposed to walk students through the process of solving a problem or finding information, rather than just handing them the answer. If a student is struggling with a math problem, for example, the feature may prompt them to refresh their memory about the rules for dividing exponents, instead of spitting out a number.

In response to the backlash, Google pointed out in a post on X that it had listened to educators by turning off access to AI products by default, and noted that schools could turn on Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search individually.

“We know there’s concern about students using AI to shortcut schoolwork, and schools have told us they want control,” Google wrote in a statement. “That’s exactly why we are making these changes today to address the feedback we’ve heard from educators in recent months. And we’ll continue to engage deeply with educators to ensure we are giving schools more choice, more controls, and improved Search for learning.”
